**CHAPTER 3**

**trimming**

I use a right angle trim tool

**trimming pots**

When you're first learning to throw, you may find it challenging to create a full-bellied, narrow-footed form with ideal wall thickness and clay evenly distributed throughout the wall; your first pots are likely to be rather bottom-heavy and in need of a trimming. Other pots that usually need trimming are bowls and other full-bellied forms, which are usually thrown with thicker walls so they won't slump on the wheel, or later, as they dry. Once the walls have firmed up, you can carve away their heaviness and bring forth a lighter, more balanced form. Similarly, some forms like narrow-footed bowls, teapots, vases, and lids can't be fully realized on the wheel; they all need to be thrown, then trimmed.

The best time to trim is when the pot has dried to the leather-hard stage. At this stage of dryness, you can handle the pot without deforming it. It's firm enough to alter, cut, or add appendages; cool to the touch; and visibly damp. You'll know if the clay you're trimming is too soft if it clumps on the edge of the trim tool; it's too hard when the tool chatters against the clay.

Variety of trimming tools;

Use thumb to finish the simplest pots

**THUMBING OFF**

The thumbing off method is a quick and simple way to finish off the base, or foot, of a leather-hard flat-bottomed pot—one that was thrown more or less exactly as you intend it to stay. If the pot's walls are of a consistent thickness from the base up to its lip, and if the floor and walls are the correct thickness, so that no surplus clay needs to be removed with a tool, then this is a good method to use. The only tools needed are a moist sponge and your fingers.

Place your leather-hard pot upside down in the center of a clean wheel head, on a ware board, or other flat surface. Holding the pot firmly with your left hand, use your right thumb to smooth and round the edge of the base. Try to do this all the way across one-half of the bottom's circumference (see left). Switch the action to your other hand and do the same for the other half.

**WHEEL TRIMMING SETUP**

No matter how your pot's going to be trimmed, you must first center it on the wheel head and secure it there. Centering ensures that the pot's wall can be trimmed to a consistent thickness. (If the pot is off center you'll remove more clay from one side of it than the other, and its foot ring will be off center, too.)

I'll show two ways to center your pots, and two options for how to secure them. If you are a beginner, you'll want to secure the pot to the wheel head with wads of clay. Then, as you gain in skill and confidence, you can try the tap-centering method (see this page).

  After a pot is upside down on the wheel, you'll need to rely on your memory of its interior shape and its thickness to guide your trimming process. You should study the shape of the pot before you start to trim it! So, first, before you attach it to the wheel head (or bat), give it a cursory feel by running your fingers along the wall and floor of the pot. Getting a sense of its thickness will help you avoid cutting too deeply as you trim.

  Moisten the rim of the pot with a sponge **(1)**. With the wheel stopped, place the pot upside down as near to the center of the bat as you can. Use the wheel rings as a guide if you're working directly on the wheel head.

**1** : Moisten rim with sponge

  Start the wheel slowly turning and hold a needle tool about a third of the way down from the foot. The tip should be 2 inches (5cm) from the spinning pot **(2)**.

**2** : Sneak up on turning pot with needle tool

  Slowly move the needle tip closer to the pot—just enough to touch the pot _only_ on the side where it's most off center. Hold the tool there for at least three revolutions of the wheel, until you have a clear scratch mark in that one place on the pot's wall **(3)**.

**3** : Allow off-center pot to touch needle tool

  Stop the wheel and turn the wheel head around until the scratch is nearest you. Gently push the pot in toward the center of the wheel. Start the wheel and check to see that the pot is centered. Repeat as necessary until you've succeeded in centering the upside-down pot. The scratch mark will be removed when the pot is trimmed.

  Stick the pot to the wheel head by pressing firmly down on it. Be sure to press straight down. If you're just starting out, you'll probably want to use wadding to fix the pot more firmly to the wheel than just by its moistened rim. With your wheel stopped, curve three clay wads to fit the curvature of the pot's rim. Holding the pot firmly to the wheel head with your left hand, position the wads evenly around the rim. Compress each wad so it sticks to the wheel head or bat **(4)**. Be aware that some pots, like lids, can't be trimmed with wadding in the way, so start practicing sticking pots without it.

**4** : Secure pot with clay wads after centering

**tap-centering**

Tap-centering is the fastest, most efficient way to center your pot on the wheel, but it takes a bit more experience than the needle method. Put the pot on the wheel head or bat. Get the wheel going to a slow speed. Focus your efforts on centering the part of the pot that is approximately one-third of the way down from the pot's foot, rather than its rim.

  Take a moment to watch the pot as it turns, judging where it's most off center. Attune to the rhythm of that off-center bias. Your left index finger should be applying light downward pressure in the center of the base of the pot, and your right hand should be near the side of the pot **(1)**.

**1** : Steady uncentered pot with one finger

  Quickly and lightly tap the pot toward center as the off-center point comes around. Lighten your taps as the pot becomes more centered, until it's finally spinning quiet and true **(2)**. Press on the pot now **(3)** , so it will stick better to the wheel head. No wadding is needed.

**2** : Move pot to center with incremental taps

**3** : Press pot to stick moistened rim to bat

**TRIMMING POTS ON THE WHEEL**

The idea of cutting into your successfully thrown pot might seem daunting, but you can gain confidence by using the proper body posture, correct hand positions, and one good, sharp trimming tool. Avoid the temptation to load up on lots of different trimming tools: use one tool until you know it well. I use a simple but effective right-angle trim tool. It can be used anywhere on the form—even the hard-to-get-to areas, like where an underbelly meets the corner of a pedestal-type foot ring.

The most common problem beginners have when learning to trim is that they cut too deep—right through the bottoms of their pots. You might trim a little, take the pot off the wheel, feel for thickness, and then re-center the pot to continue the trimming.

  To trim the bottom of a pot, moisten the bat or wheel head and center your pot. Once you are sure the pot is centered, exert even, downward pressure on it to secure the pot in place **(1)**.

**1** : Tap-center and secure pot

  Use your sharp trimming tool to take excess clay from the wall at the base of the pot **(2)**. Your left fingers remain in contact with the center of the foot, but should not exert enough pressure to slow the wheel, keeping the pot in place on the wheel head. Your left thumb braces your right hand, holding the tool close to its cutting edge.

**2** : Start trimming at base

  Gradually bring the tool down along the wall **(3)**. When you're satisfied with the wall's thickness and overall profile, make a subtle bevel where the foot meets the wall **(4)**. Resting on a table, the pot's shadow lends a sense of lift. Thumb off the bevel's edge with your right index finger. Your left finger will keep the right finger in one place if you brace the two as shown in photo **5**.

**3** : Move down wall

**4** : Bevel foot

**5** : Thumb off

**cross-section**

Beginners tend to make pots that are on the heavy side, but that's quite normal. As you practice, the idea is to evenly distribute the clay throughout the pot, so it won't have any weak areas. For example, you don't want a pot with a hefty bottom and a thin, flimsy wall. You want the clay distribution to be such that the pot is strong and balanced.

A good way to learn more about the pot's structural elements (like wall thickness, curvature, or depth of the foot) is to occasionally cut a trimmed pot vertically. It teaches you about the history of your efforts. Did you pull the wall consistently? Was the foot trimmed so that the wall is an even thickness all around? Does the pot's interior curve more or less mirror the exterior one? A cross-sectioned pot helps you identify areas for further skill development.

In the photo below, the untrimmed leather-hard pot on the left reveals the raw story of floor and wall thickness, base width, and lip curve. A similarly shaped bowl on the right has been trimmed. Its curved interior is reflected by the profile of the exterior wall—especially at the base, where the form sweeps through the narrowed foot.

Untrimmed bowl (left); trimmed bowl with full foot ring (right)

**FOOT RINGS**

While throwing your pot, you may have left extra clay in the base and floor to be trimmed away when the pot became leather-hard. Now you're ready to give the form a graceful shape and some lift by adding a foot ring. I'll demonstrate two styles for creating a foot ring on a tea bowl, so you can see the effect each one can have on the final form.

No matter what type of pot you're trimming, the basic parts of a foot ring are the same. What differs from pot to pot are the proportions of the foot ring's height, width, and diameter, relative to the pot's overall size. When you're ready to get down to trimming your pots, you'll want to think about proportion, think about the diameter of the foot in relation to the overall diameter, and think about the depth of the foot in relation to the total depth.

**FULL FOOT RING**

A full foot ring is established when you trim a pedestal at the base of the pot. (Remember, your pot is sitting upside down on the wheel, with its base facing up.) To establish the width of the foot ring, you'll trim a recess into the base itself and bevel the ring's sharp outer edge. The center of the base is then trimmed into a dome- like shape, and finally the inner edge of the foot ring is also beveled.

In most cases, your objective is to trim your pot's exterior profile so that it mirrors the interior one. As you can see in the cutaway photo at left, the curve that was cut into the base of the foot ring is simply a continuation of the wall's overall curvature.

  Your seat at the wheel is at 6 o'clock, and you'll be trimming the pot at 4 o'clock. Start the wheel spinning at a moderate speed. Press your left index finger firmly down in the center of the revolving pot.

  Hold the tool in your right hand, being sure to grip it as shown and leaving enough room at the top of the handle so you can press your left thumb there. If you're not using wads of clay, keep your left index finger firmly pressed against the center of the pot's base. Using moderate pressure at the corner area of the tool, carve into the exterior wall, just below its flat base **(1)**.

**1** : Start initial trimming at base

  Gradually bring the tool down to the underside of the belly, shaving away clay as you go. Make sure you brace your tool hand at all times. Don't cut too deeply.

  Flip the head of the tool around. Try to make the foot ring ¼ to ⅜ inch (6 to 10mm) tall. Use one point of it to establish a shallow groove for the height of the pedestal **(2)**. Deepen the groove by following this first mark.

**2** : Establish pedestal's height with tool's point

  Bevel the outermost edge of the foot ring, holding the tool as shown in photo **3**.

**3** : Bevel base of pedestal

  To establish the width of the foot ring, flip the tool over (so its point aims at your left index finger). Carve a wide, V-shaped groove inside the foot ring **(4)**.

**4** : Cut inner foot ring with tool's point

  Flip the tool back over and cut from the center out, toward the inner side of the foot ring. As you trim, aim to continue the curve of the outside wall all the way through the foot ring, so as to reflect the interior shape of the tea bowl. Hold the tool's edge at the angle shown in photo **5**. Bevel the inside edge of the foot ring.

**5** : Dome base's center

  To remove the pot, first stop the wheel. Remove the wads (if you are using them) and dislodge the pot by tapping on its side **(6)**. (If you're trimming a group of same-sized pots, remove only one or two of the wads, slip the next piece into place on the wheel, then reapply the wadding.)

**6** : Unseat pot from wheel head with tap

Trimming a full foot ring

**INNER FOOT RING**

  To trim an inner foot ring into the base of a tea bowl, first pare away the clay from the foot by moving the tool down by the side of the pot **(1)**. Next, follow the instructions for cutting the _inside_ of a full foot ring of a tea bowl on this page.

**1** : Refine lower part of tea bowl

  The two tea bowls in photo **2** were thrown to the same size, but the one on the right was trimmed with a full foot ring and the one on the left with an inner foot ring. Seeing the finished results side by side demonstrates what a difference trimming can make.

**2** : Inner foot ring (left); full foot ring (right)

**stamping pots**

If you want to make your personal mark, or seal, on the pot, this is a good time to do it. Support the interior floor, just on the other side of where the seal will be, with a middle finger. Press the seal gently into the clay. Rock it slightly, so it impresses the clay cleanly **(1)**. For more about making and using seals, see this page in the Decorating and Glazing chapter.

**1** : Press bisque-fired seal into bottom of pot

**LIDS**

Although you measured your lid when you first threw it, occasionally it won't fit the intended pot exactly. In that case, you will need to trim for fit as well as for shape. Once the lid is trimmed, you can attach a strap handle or a knob of some kind; in fact, you'll create a relationship between the handle and the lid. No matter what kind of handle you choose, always try to find what is easy on the eye, but also what is practical.

A single style of pot lid can be very versatile. My simplest lid is thrown upside down, like a plate. The rim sits down in the gallery of a pot like a casserole dish. A simple lid like this needs little in the way of trimming, and is soon ready for you to add a knob or a handle.

A variation on this basic lid form is to throw it with enough extra clay for a flange. This short wall keeps the lid securely in the pot. Naturally, a flanged lid is trimmed a bit differently than a simple one, but it, too, can take either a knob or a strap handle, according to your plan.

The cap lid for my teapot is thrown like a short, shallow cylinder. It fits over the pot's flanged rim and can be trimmed in one of two ways. Trimming all three lid types will be demonstrated here.

**SIMPLE LID FOR A CASSEROLE**

  Set the untrimmed lid into the casserole's mouth, to see how it fits **(1)**. If the lid's diameter is too large, lightly sponge the base and center it on the wheel head. Press down on the lid to secure it there. Use your trim tool to very lightly skim off the excess **(2)**.

**1** : Check initial fit of untrimmed lid in pot

**2** : Reduce diameter if need be

  Once the lid fits, you're ready to trim its top side. First, lightly moisten its edge and the wheel head. Place the lid face down on the wheel and center it (use the tap-centering technique described in the sidebar on this page). Set the wheel to moderate speed and use your index fingers to depress the center of the lid **(3)**. This shallow depression creates more space, so that a hand and perhaps a pot holder will be able to fit around a strap handle. (If you prefer a knob, you don't need to make the depression.)

**3** : Gently depress center of lid

  With the trim tool, shape the lid so that it has a dome-like profile that complements the pot's curve. Work your way up the side from the lip, to the place where the profile flattens off **(4)**. If you want to add a knob to this lid, stop here and go to this page.

**4** : Give lid a dome profile

  Holding a round-edged metal rib in both hands, firmly press down into the center of the flattened area; shave away the clay to achieve a slightly concave dip in the lid **(5)**.

**5** : Trim center with rib

  Neatly tidy up the place where the dome's curve meets the concave dip. With the trim tool and your finger, as shown in photo **6**.

**6** : Refine break point with trimming tool

**FLANGED LID FOR A CASSEROLE**

The excess clay that supported the flanged lid while it was being thrown, and as it dried, is trimmed in the same way as for a gallery-style lid. Since you'll be applying pressure to the flange, make sure it's stiff enough to withstand it. Moisten the flange lip, center the lid, and secure it to the wheel with a little pressure **(1)**.

**1** : Moisten flange with sponge

  Start trimming at the base and move down the wall toward the lip **(2)**. As your tool travel's down, shift the position of your left hand. Don't apply too much pressure. The lid should glide under your left hand. Now the lid is ready for any style of handle or knob.

**2** : Do a simple trim

**FLANGED TEAPOT AND CAP LID**

Before you can trim the base of any pot that has a flanged lip, you must first dress its flange. Often the edge, or face, of a flange will have a bit of unevenness, but the pot's base can't be trimmed as it stands upside down on its flange unless it's perfectly level. I tap-center and hold the pot to the wheel head with moisture (this page), but you can always use the extra insurance of wadding, if you prefer.

  Bracing arms and hands, hold the tool horizontally to the flange's face **(1)**. A thin flange is easily damaged, so remove the clay by small degrees with a sharp tool. In this demonstration I used two tools with different head angles, but one or the other alone will do.

**1** : Dress face of flange with trimming tool

  Turn the teapot over and ready it for trimming just as you would any other pot. Trim a bit of clay off the wall near the base, to refine the shape, narrow the foot, and lighten the weight a bit more **(2)**. I like to give my teapots a shallow full foot ring; for a more thorough explanation of how that's done, see this page.

**2** : Invert pot and trim outer base

  Like the teapot, the lip of the lid must be leveled before it can be turned over and trimmed. Trimming ensures that the cap lid has a good fit and that it won't rattle loosely on the teapot's flange. (I sometimes use this opportunity to reduce the lid's depth, too.) There are two ways to secure the lid in preparation for trimming. For the first, center and secure the teapot to the wheel, right side up, then place the lid, upside down, onto the pot's mouth. Center it. As you steady the lid with your left index finger, bevel the inner edge of the lid, so when it sits on the teapot its edge will match the slope of the teapot's shoulder **(3)**. The second method is to trim the lid while it's directly on the wheel head, as you would any other pot **(4)**.

**3** : One way to position lid for trimming

**4** : . . . Or stick cap lid to bat to trim

  When you're satisfied with the lid's fit, turn it upside down and secure it to the wheel head by moistening the rim. Be sure to press down on the center of the lid so it will stick to the wheel head. Use the trim tool to curve the outer wall slightly **(5)**. Lightly trim a slightly domed shape onto the top of the lid **(6)**.

**5** : Lightly curve lid's wall

**6** : Trim slight dome shape into top of lid

**adding a knob**

You can add a knob onto any type of trimmed lid while it's still on the wheel. A word of caution: when attaching a knob onto a flanged lid, make sure the lid is leather-hard. You'll be applying a moderate amount of pressure to the flange and don't want the lid to collapse.

  To make a knob, pinch off a small amount of soft, fresh clay **(1)** ; add or subtract clay as needed. Compare the size of the knob to the lid **(2)**. Roll the clay into a smooth ball.

**1** : Pinch off clay for knob

**2** : Estimate knob's proportion to lid

  With the wheel turning slowly, use the tip of your trimming tool to score a small area in the center of the lid **(3)**. Stop the wheel and apply a small amount of water to the scored area **(4)**. Just a few drops should do!

**3** : Score center of lid

**4** : Moisten scored section

  Position the clay for the knob onto the scored area. Use your fingertip to blend its base into the lid **(5)**. Be consistent all the way around. Get your fingers wet, start the wheel, and compress the clay down onto the lid with the tips of your first two fingers **(6)**. Support the side of the knob with your left thumb and middle finger.

**5** : Attach clay

**6** : Moisten and compress knob

  Once the clay is firmly attached, center and shape it. Do the shaping with your right index or little finger. Support that pressure with your index and thumb **(7)**.

**7** : Center and shape knob

  Compress the knob and shape the side with a downward-curving angle **(8)**.

**8** : Compress and refine side

  Finish the knob with your trimming tool **(9)**. Make it clean and crisp.

**9** : Angle-trim top only

**CHAPTER 4**

**assembling**

Handles

Assembling Complex Forms

Pulling a handle

**handles**

Assembling is the art of combining individually made parts to make up a whole, the sum of which is greater than its parts. Pulling and attaching handles take a bit of knack, so keep practicing. When a handle is made and attached properly, it looks very natural, like it might have grown right out of the pot, and it will be strong enough to easily lift the weight of the filled pot.

Here I'll show you how to make a basic pulled handle and the various assembly methods I like to use for a tankard, a pitcher, and the handles (both a strap and a lug-type) for the casserole and its lid. You can change the appearance of a handle a great deal just by giving it a little tweak, a little lift here, a little push there. Look at the part as you're attaching it to your pot and think about proportion and size. (You don't want to have a handle that looks or feels awkward or cumbersome.)

Once you've trimmed your pots and made the necessary appendages, you're ready to start assembling.

Attaching a handle;

**PULLING HANDLES**

The basic process for creating a pulled handle is shown here. I like to attach handles to a whole ware board of leather-hard pots in a single session, so for the sake of efficiency, I pull a long handle that can be cut down into several individual handles.

  Knead 1 to 2 pounds (0.5 to 0.9kg) of clay and roll it into a spike shape. Grasp it just below the top and slap the top of it with your other hand, to splay it like the head of a railroad spike **(1)**. Hold the clay by its head and dip it into a bucket of water—but not so deep that your fingers get wet. If they do, you won't be able to keep a grip on the clay. Wet your free hand.

**1** : Splayed end of clay "spike"

  Gradually stretch the wet clay by gently but quickly and smoothly pulling down along and right off the end of the tail **(2)**. Don't stop at the end or a lump will develop there. Aim to create a long, tapering handle. Pull the clay several times. Your hand should glide smoothly and quickly. Never squeeze the clay too tightly, or it might get too thin or even tear.

**2** : Pull to narrow and lengthen clay

  Rotate the pulled clay, make two or three more pulls, then rotate it back to its original position in your hand. Do this throughout the handle-pulling process, until it's 18 inches (46cm) long.

  Once the clay starts to take on the shape of a handle, hold your fingers in a more oval-like shape, as shown in photo **3**.

**3** : Reposition fingers to create oval

  Continue pulling lightly and quickly **(4)**. If you were to cut a cross-section of the pulled clay now, it would be an oval rather than round.

**4** : Extend clay into oval profile

  Wrap your right fingers around the back of the handle and, using your right thumb, run it down the entire length of the clay, to make a groove on the left side **(5)**.

**5** : Use thumb to make first groove

  Do the same on the right side. It will take several passes to get these two grooves right. Your goal is to create a handle with a spine **(6)**.

**6** : Create second groove

  Gently drape a 6- to 8-inch (15 to 20cm) length of the tail over your right hand **(7)**. Lay that section down on a nearby tabletop or board **(8)**. Where the clay meets the edge of the board, put your right thumb on top of the handle and your index finger directly below it **(9)**.

**7** : Drape pulled clay over hand

**8** : Lay section on table

**9** : Prepare to cut handle

  Holding your right thumb perpendicular to the pulled clay, use the side of your thumb to cut the handle; make the cut as vertical as possible **(10)**. After you've pulled all the handles you need, let them stiffen, uncovered, for 40 minutes or so (depending on the humidity level in the studio) before attaching them to any pots.

**10** : Thumb-cut handle at table's edge

**TANKARD HANDLE**

To attach your pulled handle to a tankard, start by gathering together a bucket of water, a small sponge, a banding wheel, and a clean ware board. Decide how you want the handle to be positioned and where you will attach it to your pot.

  Dip your thumb in the water; let a bit of water run down your thumbnail as you score the mug just under the rim **(1)**. The water will create just the right amount of slip needed to attach the handle. Put the mug on the banding wheel.

**1** : Score top attachment point

  To release the handle from the ware board, don't pick it up by its tail; instead, release it by using your thumb to push the thicker end of the handle away from you. Holding it as shown, use your thumb's knuckle to splay and widen the end of the handle **(2)**.

**2** : Splay end of handle with knuckle

  With your left hand supporting the lip of the mug on the inside, attach the thicker end of the handle to the scored area on the mug with gentle but firm pressure **(3)**.

**3** : Push handle straight onto attachment point

  Use the tip of your right thumb to blend the top side of the splayed end of the handle into the mug's wall **(4)** ; use your right index finger on the underside to do the same.

**4** : Blend handle's topside to attach

  Once you've blended and smoothed the attachment, hold the mug horizontally so that the handle hangs from the mug. Dip the handle and your free hand in the water bucket **(5)**. Be sure to support the handle as you do this maneuver.

**5** : Dip handle in water bucket

  Make two or three light pulls to freshen up and soften the handle a little **(6)**. If you want the handle to have a spine down its length, use the tip of your right thumb to reinstate it **(7)**.

**6** : Refresh handle with light pulls

**7** : Reestablish handle's spine

  Now, supporting the end of the handle, let it curve down gently, while at the same time turning the mug into a vertical position. Use your right thumb and index finger to gently stick the tail of the handle into position on the mug **(8)**. Don't push hard until you're certain about its placement. Looking at the handle straight on, make sure it's aligned with the mug **(9)**.

**8** : Lightly stick end of handle

**9** : Check handle's vertical alignment

  Tidy up the upper attachment before dealing with the tail **(10)**. When you're satisfied with the location of the handle's lower attatchment, use the right side of your right thumb to blend the right half of the handle into the mug. Start at the center of the handle and blend out, to the right **(11)**. Don't be hesitant.

**10** : Smooth underside of attachment

**11** : Thumb off right side of handle's end

  Turn the mug upside down, and use the same technique for the left half **(12)**. Flick off the tail with your right thumb, in one quick move **(13)**.

**12** : Flip mug to thumb off other side

**13** : Tear off handle's tail in one motion

  Blend and finish the tail, using only your fingers. Don't use a sponge or tool; they will spoil the clean, crisp finish on the naked clay **(14)**.

**14** : Finish only with your thumb

**PITCHER HANDLE**

Pulling, placing, and attaching a pitcher handle is similar to making one for a tankard. This demonstration shows how the handle's thickness, length, and placement differ from those used on smaller forms.

  After you've thumbed off the base of the pitcher, determine where on its lip the handle will be attached; naturally, it should be directly opposite the pouring lip **(1)**. Have a bucket of warm water ready.

**1** : Visually determine connection point

  Attach a pulled handle to the rim, using the techniques shown on this page, but attaching it at the rim rather than below it.

  Smooth the underside of the joint with your right index finger. Support the handle with your left hand **(2)**.

**2** : Use side of finger to blend underside

  Smooth the top side of the joint with your right thumb. Your right index finger supports the handle from underneath **(3)**.

**3** : Smooth top side of attachment point

  Smooth and secure the left side of the handle. Your left hand should continue to support the tail of the handle **(4)**.

**4** : Smooth left side too

  Hold the pitcher gently in your left hand. Support the handle with your right hand as you prepare to dip the handle into the water **(5)**. Dip the handle, then refresh the spine.

**5** : Support handle while moving pitcher

  Just when you've determined the handle's shape, and where the lower point of attachment will be, shift the base into position as shown in photo **6** , so you can make sure the handle is aligned to the axis of the pouring lip. Use your right index finger and thumb to lightly press the tail to the base of the pitcher.

**6** : Check overall alignment before proceeding

  Use a gentle curving motion of your index finger to refine the shape and smooth underneath the top of the handle where it attaches to the pot **(7)**.

**7** : Smooth attachment's underside

  Support the wall with your left hand inside the pot, then finish the attachment process.

  Finally, smooth the upper joint **(8)**. Refine the handle shape carefully. Check the shape of the handle, and whether it feels good in the hand **(9)**.

**8** : Use light touch for any last blends

**9** : Refine curve and check feel

**LIDDED CASSEROLE HANDLES**

To get a casserole lid ready for a pulled, strap-style handle, I make a slight depression in its center and then trim that area with a rib. The whole form will have a low, neat profile but there will still be enough space under the handle for your hand. **assembling complex forms**

Now you have everything you need to bring all your clay-working skills together on more complex pieces. In this next section, I'll show you how to join spouts and lugs to the teapot and also how to assemble a trio of GP bowls into a neat and versatile serving piece.

**ASSEMBLING A TEAPOT**

A teapot is made of many parts, separately thrown and then assembled. It should feel well balanced in your hand, pour well, and be pleasing to the eye. It can be challenging to make a teapot that is both beautiful and that functions well (i.e., it not only doesn't dribble but pours beautifully, the lid stays put while you pour, and the handle feels right and looks good). While there is no formula that can precisely dictate how this sort of harmony is found, there are some simple things you can do that will help you achieve these goals.

The quality of the individual parts you create make all the difference. A spout that is too large in relation to the body will make the teapot's overall proportions look questionable. Before you sit down to make your teapot, you might want to look at lots of examples. Then, do a lot of making. Throw many bodies, spouts, lids, and handles, then mix and match these parts to find the best relationships.

**clay moves**

Understanding how clay behaves is essential to teapot assembly. When I was young, I remember watching my father assemble a teapot in the studio at Lowerdown. He was slicing the tip of the spout at an angle that didn't look right to me, but when the teapot emerged from the warm kiln the spout had somehow righted itself into the correct position for pouring. I quickly learned that a clay spout not only shrinks during firing, but it also _twists_. You will come to notice these types of behaviors in the forms you make, and I'm sure you'll integrate those findings into your work.

**decorative techniques**

Potters have been at it a very long time and since the beginning have used decoration to help tell stories on vessels. All sorts of materials and techniques can be used to decorate pots—so many, in fact, that the array of choices might be overwhelming. Pots can be decorated at different times in their development from freshly thrown or leather-hard to bisque fired, and this chapter introduces some of the most common techniques for decorating or glazing at any stage.

From making impressions in soft clay to brush ing engobes onto leather-hard pots, to dipping bisque-fired pots in glaze, there is surely a technique shown in this chapter that will appeal to you.

A glazed, fluted pot;

A glazed, paddled pot;

Paddling, incising, and faceting tools for decoration

**IMPRESSING TECHNIQUES**

The practice of stamping or impressing patterns and imagery into the surfaces of pots seems to have started 12,000 to 15,000 years ago. You only have to stamp one of your own pots for the first time in order to understand something about our ancient impulse to leave a mark . . . and then another.

Impressions are usually made between the time when a pot is soft and pliable or when it has stiffened up a bit. The drier a pot becomes, the less willing the clay is to take an impression. Here are a few simple tools and methods for stamping freshly thrown pots that are still attached to the wheel head or bat.

**PADDLING**

Paddling leaves an impression in a freshly thrown pot. The wooden paddle has a three-dimensional design carved into it, which, when whacked into the surface of a pot, transfers the design from the paddle to the pot.

The paddle can be used in several different ways, but the timing of the process is important. It's easier to leave a deep impression in the soft clay of a freshly thrown pot than it is in a leather-hard or stiff one. On the other hand, a wet pot sometimes sticks to the paddle. To achieve the desired depth and crispness, practice the technique outlined here on a bellied form.

  Leave your just-thrown pot on the bat and use your throwing stick to remove the slip **(1)**. Less slip on the surface leaves it less sticky and better able to hold the design.

**1** : Remove slip

  Soak the paddle in water for a couple of minutes first, to keep the wet clay of the freshly thrown pot from adhering to the paddle's carved design **(2)**.

**2** : Soak paddles

  Put your hand inside the pot, directly behind the area where you intend to paddle. Press your fingers tightly together, touching the wall. Aim a quick, short stroke directly at the supported area of the wall, pulling the paddle straight off the clay without letting it turn or twist in your hand **(3)**.

**3** : Press or strike pot with paddle

  With the wheel turning moderately fast, reshape the lip in the same way you might finish throwing it. Brace your hands—don't let the misshapen form push your hands around.

**CUTTING TECHNIQUES**

Another way to decorate a pot is to cut into the surface. This can be done by faceting or carving into the pot at various stages of drying, from freshly thrown to leather-dry.

**FACETING**

Faceting is the art of cutting planes into the surface of a pot. If you cut facets into a freshly thrown one, the facets may be crisp but the just-cut planes are still soft and supple. You might try wetting only the interior of the pot and, without touching its exterior, push outward, so the form expands and gives a more natural, flowing quality to each facet. If instead you choose to wait for the pot to stiffen to the leather-hard stage, the facets you cut are more likely to be sharp, smooth, and precise. Try experimenting with pots at different stages of dryness.

You can facet with almost anything that has an edge sharp enough to slice through clay. Some potters like to use wire tools, braided steel or nylon, or perhaps a cheese slicer, on leather-hard clay. Another option is a kinked guitar string, which I quite like. In this demonstration, I faceted the pot right after it was made on the wheel. A curly wire made one set of facets whereas a straight wire was used on the neighboring planes. The contrast between the surfaces created a dynamic aesthetic.

The broader the facets you intend to cut, the thicker the wall needs to be. I started with a freshly thrown, thick-walled pot and ribbed the exterior wall to remove the slip, for a clean surface. The base of the pot has been beveled but not yet cut from the wheel.

  Use a kinked or curly wire. Hold it taut, with your hands spaced a little wider than that of the facet you intend to cut. Bracing both wrists on the wheel and with the wire held taut, start each facet with the wire positioned on top of the lip **(1)**. As you cut, stay aware of the wall's thickness and curve. Try to follow that curve all the way.

**1** : Cut facets with curly wire

**FLUTING**

Fluting is a type of surface decoration made by carving away clay using a sharp tool. Timing the fluting to the wetness of your pot is a matter of preference and experience. When the clay is soft, loop tools are best for getting deep, rounded flutes. With a drier pot, fluting becomes more of a carving exercise with angular or shallow flutes. Here, I use a broken-off hacksaw blade, which I sharpened on a grindstone. One end is rounded and the other squared off.

  On a leather-hard teapot, start the fluting to one side of the spout. Using the rounded end of the blade, direct the carving stroke away from you and toward the base of the pot. Each flute is positioned relative to the previous one, allowing minor differences in line quality so that the pattern has a hand-drawn aesthetic **(1)**.

**INCISING**

Directly carving a design or motif into the surface of a pot is called incising. I think the best results are achieved on leather-hard clay when the motif can stand out sharp and clear. Compared to the flutes cut into the planes of a pot (see Fluting, this page), the marks made in the drier clay have sharper edges. Be sure to brush off the burrs from your "drawing" before you fire the pot. Each tool leaves its unique mark, so experiment with different tools. After incising, the pot can be bisque fired and then either finished with a translucent glaze, to let the design show through, or left unglazed and stony-looking.

  To incise a leather-hard pot, I like to use a lemon zester, which creates groups of parallel lines. Draw the tool toward you **(1)**. Incise a vertical row of triangular flecks between each row of lines with the sharp tip of a hacksaw blade or other sharp trimming tool **(2)**.

**INLAY**

Inlay technique is the process of incising, or cutting into, leather-hard clay with a tool, and then filling the void with a contrasting slip, or perhaps an engobe (see this page). The excess is then scraped off with a sharp rib, revealing a clean-edged motif. Plan to apply inlay when the clay is the right degree of semi-stiffness: too soon, and the design won't be crisp; too dry, and the inlay material can flake off or fall out of the incision later. Thin incisions tend to work best. The incisions on the stoneware bottle in this demonstration were filled with my own porcelain-based formulation.

Use any kind of tool that will make the sort of pattern you envision. Standard pottery tools, dental tools, woodworking tools—anything strong enough to carve into stiff clay will work. Each tool leaves a mark of its unique character in the lines and shapes you make with it. After the incised and inlaid pot is fully dry, bisque fire it. You might want to then cover the pot with a translucent glaze, so the motif can be seen through the glassy surface. Or fire the pot to a high temperature without any glaze at all. This gives a dry, geological look to the pot. Opaque glazes would hide or obscure the incising, but you can always experiment.

**ENGOBES**

In its simplest form, engobe is little more than a creamy slip, like the slurry you remove from a thrown pot before you take it off the wheel (which is why many potters refer to engobe as "slip"). The difference between the two is mainly the amount of non-plastic (not for throwing) materials in the mixture. In the right proportions, a fluxing (melting) agent and other ingredients make the engobe more vitreous. (The more vitreous an engobe is, the more it resembles a glaze.) Engobe can be used to decorate a pot from the time it's freshly thrown and still on the wheel to when it's almost dry.

Engobe can be an attractive alternative to glaze. Because it is made of mostly clay, it has a high melting point (like the pot it covers), and that makes it possible to paint fine lines that won't blur when fired. You can use a commercial product (it's available in lots of colors), or mix a batch of your own base recipe and add colorants of your own choosing (see this page).

Non-plastic clays are often part of an engobe recipe, and the ratio of all the ingredients in its formulation must be balanced, and also suitable for the shrinkage rate of the clay you used to make your pot. To the whitish base recipe you might add a colorant: an oxide, a stain, or a carbonate. The more flux an engobe recipe has, the more intense its coloring agents become; the colors in low-melt (that is, more slip-like) engobes tend to be more muted.

Whether commercially made or "from scratch," engobes are formulated for the three major firing temperatures:

cone 04 (1945°F / 1063°C)

cone 6 (2232°F / 1222°C)

cone 10 (2345°F / 1285°C)

**colorants**

A colorant is a dry ingredient that you add to a mixed base formula. Being inorganic in origin, a colorant is the "spice" in a recipe: with some you use a lot, and others only a little; it depends. The amount of colorant that will go into a base mixture is expressed as a percentage of the recipe's total volume. For example, to 100 grams of the base recipe, you might add, say, 3 percent (i.e., 3 grams) of chrome oxide, which is a colorant used to obtain a chrome green. (The same rule applies to any glaze recipe that you mix yourself.)

The manufactured material that can be used to give color to an engobe, in amounts from 5 to 18 percent, is called a stain. Stains are fired combinations of various oxides, silica, and fluxes, and are consistent and reliable, though some aren't suitable for temperatures higher than cone 6, or for a reduction atmosphere. Stains containing cadmium, selenium, vanadium, and praseodymium usually produce dynamic variations on yellow, orange, and red. If you are firing to high temperatures, or in a reduction atmosphere, ask your supplier if the stain you plan to use is appropriate. Find out more about colorants on this page.

Mixing pigments on glazed tiles

**glazes**

Glaze is essentially a combination of materials that, when heated enough, fuses with the clay pot surface, melts, and then cools to a hard—though not necessarily shiny—finish. The process of glazing is possibly the most complex element in the art of pottery. After all, it's in the glaze and subsequent firing where the greatest number of mineral oxides interact, creating endless variations in the finished results.

Mastering the technique of glazing requires a bit of practice. There are commercial, premixed glazes that you can use with sure results. But at some point, you might wonder what is actually in a glaze. What causes the depth of a particular color? Can I create my own custom glaze? Creating your own glaze is a satisfying pursuit that combines geology, mathematics, chemistry, and creativity. It's also a fun way to expand your decorative repertoire. You can follow a glaze formula to create your own, which isn't that different than working with a recipe in the kitchen (see this page for recipes).

Glazes are comprised of mineral oxides that are quarried and mined, just like clay. Glaze recipes require three essential types of oxides: fluxes, stabilizers, and glass formers. Common fluxes are sodium, potassium, and calcium; these lower the melting points of materials like silica and alumina. A glaze needs a stabilizer like alumina or boric oxide to regulate the melting glaze's flow and viscosity; either of these gives body to the glaze. (Boric oxide is also a glass former and strong flux.) Silica is the main glass former in both glass and glaze.

Glazed stoneware bud vases decorated with a variety of engobes and on-glaze colorants;

A bottle that has been glazed using the wax resist technique

Most glazes also contain either ball clay or kaolin, which suspends the liquid glaze in the bucket, helps a glaze bond to the pot, provides silica and alumina for the glass and body structure of the glaze, and adds to the glaze's durability. Having clay in a glaze formula makes the surface harder, less dusty, and easier to paint an additional colorant on the dry glaze surface before firing it.

Glazes come in an endless variety of finishes but the main types are glossy, satin, and matte. A glossy glaze on the interior of a functional pot is sometimes called a "liner," and it makes dishwashing easier. Satin glazes are soft to the touch, though some scratch easily. Matte glazes have a dry look; most don't run when melted, so they're ideal for painting patterns or images. You can combine multiple glazes on one pot. For example, apply a glaze that melts aggressively over a less melty matte one to create beautiful color blends and fields.

A glaze is sometimes described by how much light can pass through it. The three most common light-refracting characteristics are transparent, translucent, and opaque. A transparent glaze is clear and glossy; it has enough flux to thoroughly melt all the other materials but no opacifiers or other coloring oxides in its formula. Translucent glazes vary from clear to somewhat opaque (due to the presence of colorants or opacifiers). The more opaque glazes can have a satin or matte finish.

A glaze coating can be decorative in itself, or a vehicle for some sort of decoration. Either way, glaze always interacts with the clay underneath it. Their relationship is called the clay body-glaze interface. For instance, if you paint a motif on a pot using an engobe and then cover the pot with a glaze, there will surely be an interaction when the piece is fired. Sometimes it's a subtle one, allowing the lines to remain crisp. Other times, if the engobe is vitreous enough, and the glaze melts enough, the coloring oxides in the engobe are drawn up into the glaze. Highly fluxed engobes bleed into the glaze. On-glaze colorants are also a great way to add marks, images, or motifs to the top of a layer of glaze; the result is usually soft-edged lines.

Glaze colors are dependent upon, and influenced by, the temperatures to which the pottery is fired. A very low firing temperature (cone 018) is used to fire delicate gold and silver luster enamels. An excellent range of cherry reds, lemon-yellows, burnt-oranges and turquoise blues are possible with cone 04. Mid- and high-fire temperatures (cones 6 to 10) don't offer as much range, due to coloring oxides and high heat, but there is an unequaled depth of color.

Techniques for applying glazes to your ware, and the equipment and tools used, can be simple: pouring, dipping, brushing, spraying, and dabbing, to name more than a few. The important thing is to get the right amount of glaze on your pot for the effect that you would like. This takes experience and trial and error. Glazes can be fussy, so make sure that you keep good notes, and keep practicing!

**leach glazes**

Using high-temperature clay bodies and glazes has been a Leach family tradition dating back to the early twentieth century when my grandfather, Bernard, began making pots. However, our family has also produced earthenware pottery and I have done raku at times. My grandfather was introduced to raku when he was living in Japan and he was immediately drawn to the excitement of the process. Both my brother Johnny and I continue to use a limited palette that emphasizes a straightforward play between clay body and glaze, melding firing atmosphere, clay body, and glaze together in order to create pots that have a simple beauty, yet are very functional.

**MIXING GLAZE**

You can choose whether to use premixed commercial glaze or explore mixing your own glaze from scratch. In this section I'll show you how to get started with glaze mixing. You'll need some space for the job—though not much—and the following equipment:

  **Fine-particle respirator**

  **Scale (digital or tri-beam balance type)**

  **Clean 5-gallon (19L) buckets***

  **Clean scoops and large spoons**

  **Supply of hot water**

  **Hand drill with augur attachment**

* A two-piece sieve bucket has a fitted sieve inset; alternatively, you can hold or rest some other style of sieve over the empty bucket.

The 5-gallon (19L) plastic bucket is a standard container for glaze mixing. It can hold about 8,000 grams of dry glaze materials—plus the necessary amount of water needed for slaking (see next paragraph)—and there will still be enough room left for dipping pots into it without the contents overflowing.

You start with a formula or "recipe," which lists each ingredient as a percentage of the total (i.e., 100 percent, before any colorants are added). From the percentage, you can calculate the weight needed to make a batch of glaze. It takes about 8,000 grams of dry ingredients, plus 800 millilitres of hot water for every 1,000 grams of dry material, to fill a 5-gallon (19L) bucket.

Let's look at a glaze recipe my father, David Leach, formulated; he named it Yi Ching Celadon. On the left side of the table is his recipe, given in percentages; on the right, a factor of 40 is used to convert each percentage into the actual weight needed to fill about half the bucket. (For a full bucket of glaze, you would use a factor of 80 instead.)

**WAXING AND GLAZING**

During a firing, superheated glaze becomes tacky and sticky, then melts and becomes permanently fused to whatever it's in contact with. Wax resist protects areas of a pot from being coated with glaze, so that the piece won't fuse itself to the kiln shelf it sits on during the firing. Waxing can also be used decoratively to create lively motifs and patterns. Some typical areas to wax would be a foot, a base, or a rim. You can put wax just under the lip of a teapot spout and that tiny break in the glaze there keeps the spout from dribbling.

One last note: be sure to immediately wipe off any drops of glaze clinging to waxed areas. Just putting wax resist on a pot isn't enough to keep the glaze off that area. Remove glaze droplets from the wax coating with a damp sponge.

**WOOD ASH PATINA**

Have you ever looked at a pot that seems to be unglazed, and yet it has a most organic-looking patina? If its hues are golden, off-green, or a rich brown, chances are it's wood ash that did it. Believe it or not, that's a glaze. A tree's roots draw mineral oxides out of the ground and into their wood and bark. Firewood is used as fuel in a wood-fired kiln, the light and fluffy ash drifts through the chamber, alighting on and sticking to the pots. If the temperature gets hot enough, the ash melts.

No matter where you live, in deep forest or concrete jungle, it's possible for you to achieve a similar effect on your pots. Whether you use an electric or a gas kiln, you can make a decorative ash glaze. To make the ash, you'll need any kind of wood kindling, a garbage can lid, some paper to help get the fire started, and a metal bowl to contain the ashes.

**ON-GLAZE COLORANTS**

On-glaze colorants are mixtures of coloring oxides, flux, and sometimes a bit of clay to help flow and adhesion. These ceramic "paints" are usually mixed to a slightly more watery consistency than glaze because they are applied right on top of an unfired layer of glaze. The fired effect of on-glaze colorants usually looks more ethereal than that of an engobe or underglaze. (The engobe or underglaze is applied underneath a clear glaze, resulting in sharper detail. An on-glaze colorant melts outward into the layer of glaze, and is blurrier.)

On-glaze colorants can be used on any kind of glaze and in any type of firing. A typical recipe for an iron-red on-glaze colorant might be:

**troubleshooting on-glaze colorants**

If the brush with the colorant keeps sticking to the glaze it might be because your glaze is "dusty" (low in clay content and therefore lacking in surface hardness), so take care when you pick up glazed pots not to smudge or mar the surface. To correct the problem, you can add a gum solution to the on-glaze colorant, in the same way you would for an acrylic or oil paint. Gum is available from most ceramic supply stores. Add enough hot water to the powdered gum to make it syrupy and thick; stir until it's thoroughly dissolved. Add 1 tablespoon (15ml) of gum solution for every 100 milliliters of on-glaze colorant. Gum burns out at a low temperature and leaves no trace.

**WAX RESIST DECORATION**

Wax resist decoration is very similar to _pysanka_ (Ukrainian egg decorating) and _batik_ (a method for dyeing textiles). Wherever you apply the wax, the glaze can't stick. A waxed area on a bisque surface resists the glaze you dip the pot into. After firing, the area you waxed is left as unglazed ceramic.

Wax resist can be used at almost any stage in the production of a ceramic piece. It is possible to build up layers of glaze or on-glaze colorants by applying wax resist at different stages. You can even use wax resist on leather-hard or dry clay to develop imagery with engobes or slips.

**kilns and firing**

There are few experiences that equal the excitement potters feel when unloading glazed pots from a kiln. Nothing beats that first moment of holding your own pot and studying the qualities it has acquired in the tremendous heat of the kiln. The many changes that take place during a firing can appear mysterious and magical and at times it can seem like there's almost too much to be known. There's always something to be learned about this fascinating process, and learning from your mistakes can help you be more creative and successful.

Electric kiln;

Gas kiln;

**KILNS**

Kilns are the furnaces that potters use to fire their pots by means of applying controlled, high heat. A kiln is classified first by the fuel it uses. "Atmospheric" kilns are fired with gas (below, right), oil, or wood. In atmospheric designs, the potter adjusts dampers in order to promote various atmospheres in the chamber where the pots are being fired. Increasing the amount of air creates an "oxidation" atmosphere and reducing it creates a "reduction" atmosphere. With attention to timing, reduction produces unique (i.e., no two alike) effects on clays and glazes.

Electric kilns (below, left) generally provide an oxidation atmosphere, but the effects of the firing are more predictable. The oxidation atmosphere in an electric kiln is a result of there not being an open flame to consume oxygen molecules. The colors of fired ceramic bodies are usually lighter in oxidation than they would be after a reduction firing, and the achievable color range of glazes is greater in oxidation.

A raku kiln (shown at right) is a quick-firing, normally gas-fueled design, often made out of steel mesh and ceramic fiber blanket. The raku process involves unloading glowing red-hot pots with tongs one by one and placing them in individual containers called "reducing bins" with wood shavings or similar combustible organic matter.

With the notable exception of pit-firing, wood-fired kilns are the very oldest type of kiln and, depending on cultural traditions, can come in radically different designs.

No matter which type of kiln you use, care must be taken with its setup and usage to safeguard yourself, your studio, and the environment. Heated clays and glazes produce gases, and some of these may be toxic. Check local ordinances on emissions and related matters, and follow the kiln manufacturer's guidelines. Gas kilns need secure and of course leak-free connections on the burners and lines to their fuel tanks; electric kilns require absolutely sound wiring. All kilns must be set on concrete or other heat-resistant pads and require proper venting, as well as your watchfulness every time they're fired.

**TELLING TEMPERATURE**

A good firing is one in which the form, clay, and glaze are perfectly melded. There are an infinite number of variables that come into play during the melting of glaze materials and the vitrification of the clay itself, and you'll want as much information as possible so that this part of the ceramic process doesn't turn into a big disappointment.

The kiln's heating rate and final temperature require careful control no matter which type of kiln, clay, or glaze you use, and you'll learn a lot after you open the kiln and look inside. You can determine that the kiln has reached the right temperature in three different ways: by color, pyrometer, and cones. As a kiln gets hotter, its materials and atmosphere undergo changes in color. Judging by color takes a lot of experience; it's best to use cones or a pyrometer. Some kilns are outfitted with an electronic controller that does the analyzing and adjusting for you **(1)**. Another common approach, suitable for any kind of kiln, is using one or more pyrometric cones, which are made of refractory materials and record the heat-work that is taking place during the firing (that is, how your control of the kiln is progressing). A supplementary device, often used in conjunction with cones, is the pyrometer **(2)**.

**1** : Digital controller with pyrometer

Use a pyrometer to gauge the kiln's internal temperature—you can't open the kiln while it's firing! The pyrometer only gauges specific heat levels (though some have an oxygen probe, to assess the atmosphere), but not how the ceramic material is reacting; for that, there is the pyrometric cone. This small, pyramid-shaped device is placed in the kiln before the firing and measures the heating rate in degrees. Cones are numbered in steps, from 022 (very low temperature) up to 14 (the highest practical temperature for firing handmade ceramic pots). Earthenware clays are usually fired between cone 09 (1688°F / 920°C) and cone 02 (2016°F / 1102°C). Stoneware may be fired in the range of cones 04 to 10 (1945°F / 1063°C to 2345°F / 1285°C). Most porcelain clays are fired to temperatures between cones 6 (2232°F / 1222°C) and 10 (2345°F / 1285°C). See the pyrometric cone chart on this page.

**2** : Analog pyrometer with thermocouple

Handles and spouts would move a great deal as the pots dry and are fired. A good way to address the problem is to add percentages of grog, silica sand, or fire clay . . . or a combination of all three. Adding these materials will drive down the shrinkage rate. **CONE PACKS**

Pyrometric cones are one of several ways to monitor the firing process. Instead of setting the cone directly on a kiln shelf, you embed it at the proper angle in a wad of clay and let the clay dry.

**BISQUE FIRING**

Usually, a single cone that matches your target temperature is sufficient for a bisque firing.

  Dip a small wad of the same clay that your pots are made with into silica sand. Work the sand into the wad **(1)**. The triangular cone has been made to lean in one direction, and it will bend that way when its rated temperature is reached **(2)**. Push the cone down into the wad of clay so that it leans at the proper angle **(3)**. Don't stand the cone perfectly straight up! Use a wire or needle tool to poke holes into the clay wad **(4)**. This, too, helps evaporation. Let the clay dry thoroughly before you use it.

The cones, representing different temperatures, act as monitors for various stages in the progress of glaze firing; this is especially helpful in a reduction firing. A reduction atmosphere (gas and wood-fired kilns) requires the potter to make adjustments—based on assessments of the process as it's happening—throughout the firing. The programmed electric kiln (oxidation atmosphere) has streamlined much of the work, but you still can benefit from the feedback that only a cone pack provides. Two types of packs will be shown here: cone 10 firing and cone 04 firing.

Fired cones

When I can see through the kiln's peephole that it has bent properly, that's the signal it's time to start the reduction phase of the firing.)

When the tip touches down, the firing is finished. Cone 11 is the guard cone **(7)**. No matter what type of kiln or atmosphere you fire in, increasing the temperature much past that needed for the guard cone to bend will have negative effects on your pots.

**BISQUE AND GLAZE FIRING**

Pots are usually fired twice. Though a bare, unfired pot may look and feel dry, the first firing drives out every last vestige of water—even the kind called "chemical water"—and expels, as gas, any foreign bodies. The initial firing process transforms the clay into an irreversible ceramic state called bisque.

Each of the three major types of clay—earthenware, stoneware, and the group of high-fire clays that include porcelain—is fired to bisque by controlling the rate at which the kiln reaches the temperature necessary for that clay to become hard, yet still porous. Bisque firings can be accomplished in any kind of kiln, as long as it's done in an oxidizing atmosphere.

Bisque firings are done to lower temperatures and can take a longer time than the typically hotter glaze firing. Controlling the rate, duration, and firing temperature allows waters and gases to leave the clay without causing the damage that a quick, hot firing would do. Clay thick ness (no greater than ½ inch, or 13mm) and the degree of wetness still present also play roles in how the clay responds to the firing process.

The effective firing range needed to attain the bisque state must be adjusted for the qualities of the materials that make up the clay. The clay manufacturer will provide guidelines for a suitable firing range, but you should expect to do some testing, too. Typically during a second firing, the glaze coating becomes glass-like and fuses to the vitrified clay. Some glazes may be fired in either oxidation or reduction; others work only in one of these specifically. One example of this is a glaze that uses copper as a colorant. In reduction, it might turn red, but in oxidation the same glaze is green.

No matter what kind of pots you make, you have the option of using either a premixed (commercial) glaze or one of the glaze recipes given in this book (see this page). Keep in mind, however, that not all hand-mixed glazes are food-safe. Commercially made glazes are marked with that information.

Glazes are greatly affected by firing temperatures. Generally, the higher the firing temperature, the more limited the range of glaze colors possible. Lower-fire temperatures, used for earthenware mostly, offer a rainbow of glaze color options. The most durable pots are made with high-density clays, well fitted to their glazes, and fired to high temperatures, like cone 10.

Most modern electric kilns are equipped with a digital controller that can be easily programmed to fire the kiln. The controller utilizes segments to regulate the firing process, and each segment contains three stages. The rate of increase in the kiln's temperature is called the 1) ramp. That ramp is paired with a 2) target temperature. The third is the 3) soak, or hold. The hold is the length of time that the target temperature is to remain constant, and it allows water or gases to be driven off, or some form of heat treatment to take place. You can set a programmable electric kiln to make all these adjustments for you, though you must always attend the kiln throughout its firing process. In the case where you don't have an electric kiln with a controller and are instead using a gas or wood-fired kiln, you can always approximate a similar firing program by using the Bisque Firing Cycle at right. For this you will need a pyrometer (see more about telling temperatures on this page).

In any event, have an advance plan for what you'll do if something goes wrong. Keep fire-safety equipment nearby and practice how to use it.

As for me, I fire my glazes in three different atmospheres, to three different temperatures, to get three different results: bisque firing, high-temperature glaze firing, and raku. The first two I fire in my gas kiln. Pots made with a raku clay body get a low-temperature firing in a small gas raku kiln.

**bisque firing cycle**

Because the purpose of the first firing is to drive off residual water, all clays can be successfully bisque fired within a temperature range that is equivalent to cones 10 to 6. The peak temperature I recommend, 1670°F / 910°C, can be attained at the rate of 190°F / 105.5°C per hour (3°F / 1.6°C per minute). Monitor the rate with the pyrometer in the earlier stages of firing; the cone pack will tell the rest of the story. With so many variables at play, testing and note taking can be very helpful.

**LOADING A BISQUE KILN**

When your pots are bone-dry—not cool to the touch—they are called green ware, and they are ready to be bisque fired. Since fuel efficiency is of paramount concern, it's best to wait until your studio's shelves are filled with mugs, bowls, and jars. The tighter you can stack your green ware in the kiln, the better. In most cases, you will be able to fit more pots into a bisque firing than in a glaze firing because the unglazed pots can touch each other and even be stacked one inside another. A tightly packed kiln, full of pots and furniture that absorb and conduct heat, ensures a more even distribution, or conduction, of that heat. In gas kilns, stacking tightly is especially important because open spaces might otherwise create flame paths that would cause uneven heating. If firing with gas, make sure the burners are cleaned of any foreign matter on or near the orifices. If you're using an electric kiln, vacuum the elements. Loose debris on heating elements can cause overheating and degrade the elements more quickly.

Three posts should be spaced triangularly, so that they support two corners of the long sides of the shelf and the center of the shelf's short side. **LOADING A GLAZE KILN**

Preparation is key to loading a kiln with glazed pots. Before putting that first pot in the kiln, make sure you've cleaned the feet of your pots of any glaze so that drips don't melt and stick the pot to the kiln shelf. If you have pots with lids, remember that both the lid and its seating area must be free of glaze. Check that spouts aren't plugged with glaze. Grind off old melts and apply kiln wash to your shelving and posts (see this page). Vacuum any loose bits off the kiln floor, walls, and lid or arch; those tiny wayward pieces of kiln flotsam seem to find their way onto pots. Before you load, make any necessary cone packs and give them time to dry (see this page).

Loading a glaze firing isn't nearly the jigsaw puzzle that a bisque firing is. You won't be able to fit as many pots into the kiln this time because they shouldn't touch each other. You'll still arrange the pots in such a way that shelf space is used efficiently.

For a gas kiln, allow some air space between the tops of the pots and the shelf above them, so that gases can circulate. Use posts ½ to 1 inch (1.3 to 2.5cm) taller than the pots you plan to put on that shelf. In an electric kiln, pots and posts can be nearer to equal in height. In any event, it's a good idea to alternate the heights of shelves, to avoid creating areas of uneven heating.

**RAKU FIRING**

Of all of the firing techniques available, raku is probably the most immediately gratifying one. With the right clay body, glazes, and kiln, a pot can move from a bisque firing to a raku glaze firing and onto your table in less than an hour. While the temperatures reached in such a short time won't completely vitrify the clay body (which helps make a pot durable), this technique can result in some great decorative pieces.

During a raku firing, bisque-fired pots are usually heated to 1950°F (1066°C), or until their glazes melt. One by one, the glowing-hot pots are moved from the kiln and each one carefully placed inside a metal can (or some other airtight container), where it undergoes intense reduction because of the presence of carbonaceous material. This reduction process transforms the glazes, creating lustrous or iridescent effects, while any exposed or unglazed part of the pot usually turns a satiny black from the smoke of the burning materials. When raku firing, always take care to protect yourself from the possibility of burns. Wear heavy-duty gloves, such as those that welders use, and only remove your hot pots from the raku kiln with a good pair of raku tongs. For raku firing, you'll also need to have the following on hand:

**Bisque-fired pots.** Most commercial clay suppliers sell raku clays. While pots made from your regular clay can be raku fired, a raku clay expels water easily and is thermal-shock resistant. Bisque-fire your pots and coat them with raku glazes (see this page for a recipe) before you fire them.

**Kiln.** Any kiln that can reach 1950°F / 1066°C can be used to heat the pot prior to the raku reduction process. A small, gas-fueled fiber kiln heats pots more quickly and efficiently than does a larger one, as you probably won't want to raku fire dozens of pots in a single session.

**Reduction bins.** A suitable bin is a galvanized metal one, such as a 5–10 gallon (19–38L) garbage can. The lid should fit well; the smoke must be contained if it is to thoroughly penetrate the pot. Prepare one bin for each pot you intend to fire.

**Reduction materials.** Pretty much anything that burns and creates smoke is a "reduction material." The most popular kinds are straw, sawdust, and newspaper. Fill the reduction bin with the combustible material _before_ you put a heated pot in it.

**Tongs.** You'll need long-handled steel tongs to remove pots from a hot kiln. These are available through most ceramic suppliers.

**Leather gloves.** High-quality leather glove _s_ are an absolute must for raku. Welders' gloves are ideal and can be purchased at any good hardware store.

**Metal water bucket.** After the pots are reduced in the bins, some potters like to then place them in water momentarily so that body reduction and glaze color are stabilized. It's always a good idea to have a garden hose nearby in case of fire.

**Clothing.** Wear protective clothing because you'll be exposed to flame and smoke during the process. Never wear nylon or synthetic fabrics. A long-sleeved, cotton T-shirt, long pants, and leather shoes provide the best protection. You might want to wear a respirator during the reduction phase to filter the abundant smoke.

**BUILDING A RAKU KILN**

A raku kiln is a simple, speedy, and efficient way to glaze fire pots, and constructing your own raku kiln is relatively easy to do. Unlike an atmospheric, draft-style kiln, a raku kiln doesn't need an extended chimney to circulate air and pull out the gases.

Here's what you'll need to build a 24 x 18-inch (61 x 46cm) barrel-shaped kiln:

  **Tin snips, measuring tape, needle-nose pliers, and utility knife**

  **A sheet of steel mesh or hardware cloth that measures 24 x 100 inches (61 x 254cm). The galvanized, zinc-coated, or plain steel should be 19 gauge or heavier, and the mesh size either N inch (6mm) square or N x K inch (6 x 13mm). Don't use aluminum, which might warp or melt.**

  **40,000-BTU raku system, which includes a Venturi burner, high-pressure safety pilot valve with thermocouple, hose (K inch, or 1.3cm, in diameter), gauge, and low-pressure regulator**

  **A sheet of K23 or K26 (2 inches, or 5cm, thick) insulating fiber blanket that measures 24 x 80 inches (61 x 203cm); available from a ceramic or refractory supply dealer**

  **A fine-particle respirator with cartridges rated for the micron size of the blanket fibers and safety glasses**

  **Wooden board, 24 x 6 x O inches (61 x 15 x 2cm)**

  **20 feet (6.1m) of nichrome wire, available from a ceramic supply dealer**

  **52 two-hole ceramic buttons, each 1K inches (3.8cm) in diameter. You can make these buttons yourself out of clay and fire them to cone 06.**

  **Steel wire**

  **One or more mullite or corderite kiln shelves that measure 14 x 12 x O inches (35.6 x 30.5 x 2cm) each**

  **40- or 100-pound propane tank**
