**connecting and lighting a gas burner**

You will need to hire a licensed plumber to safely connect your kiln's burners to a fuel source. Once the burners are safely connected, follow these steps carefully to light the burners.

  **Make sure all valves leading to your burners are closed. Open your kiln's lid or door.**

  **Open the gas tank's main valve and then the valve preceding the safety shut-off valve near the burner.**

  **Use a butane lighter or light a piece of paper. Hold the flame close to the tip of the pilot burner.**

  **Depress the button on the safety shut-off valve and ignite the pilot burner. Hold the button down for one minute before releasing it.**

  **Slowly open the main burner valve until it ignites. Turn the pressure down to a low flame.**

**CONVERTING AN ELECTRIC KILN TO GAS**

If you'd like to have a gas kiln but your studio is too small or your budget too limited to buy a commercial one, you can convert an electric kiln to gas.

Any electric kiln can be modified to use LP or natural gas; you might want to purchase a used electric kiln, since even a new, smaller one is not inexpensive. Most cylindrical electric kilns have an interior volume of 5 to 20 cubic feet. The one shown in this demonstration has a volume of 9 cubic feet. To calculate the volume of this kiln design, use this formula: 3.14 x radius2 x height/depth (π x r2 x h).

Knowing your kiln's volume will help you determine the sizes of the flues and chimney you'll build with bricks, as well as the ratings of the burners needed. The "quasi-downdraft" style shown here has the chimney inside the chamber, which vents through the lid. The bottom shelf acts as the cover for an exit flue in the floor, which leads to the base of the chimney.

In the past thirty years, most electric kilns have been constructed with high-quality, low-alkali insulating firebrick (IFB), most often K23 brick. While the refractory industry recommends against using K23 brick (which is rated to 2300°F / 1260°C) for kilns that will be fired to cone 10 (2381°F / 1305°C), experience tells us that this is okay. Just don't fire a kiln built with bricks having this rating to temperatures exceeding cone 10, or they will soon start to degrade. If you're in doubt about the rating of the bricks in the kiln you're interested in, ask the manufacturer.

Electric kilns are wrapped in a thin steel skin that helps protect their relatively thin firebrick walls. If the steel skin is visible from inside the kiln, it's not safe to use anymore. It's okay if the steel on a used kiln has a bit of corrosion. Make sure the kiln's floor isn't corroded from glaze drippings, either. The lid should feel solid, and not have any cracks in it. You won't be using the electric elements, kiln sitter, or controller, so their condition isn't important.

Use a screwdriver and an adjustable wrench to remove the terminal boards, elements, controller, and any other electronic gear attached to the interior or exterior of the kiln. Most electric kilns have easily separated sections.

You'll put the sections back together after you've cut the burner ports.

Install your kiln in a well-ventilated, suitable location, on a concrete floor or pad. Allow 3 feet (1m) of clearance from all walls, and fireproof walls near the kiln with gypsum board or some other inflammable material. If you're unsure of how to fireproof the kiln area, consult a contractor. Never locate a kiln inside a living space.

Here's what you'll need:

  **Permanent marker, tape measure, tin snips, file, and chisel**

  **O-horsepower (0.56KW) electric drill**

  **K-inch (1.3cm) drill bit**

  **Respirator**

  **Keyhole saw (purchase a cheap one; you'll dull the blade by cutting brick)**

  **K26 soft-type insulating firebrick (IFB)***

  **Brick saw (needed only for HD refractory bricks)**

  **Heat-setting refractory mortar, K gallon (1.9L)**

  **Palette knife**

  **Ceramic fiber blanket (1 square foot, or 30.5cm, will be plenty)**

  **Kiln shelf made of mullite, corderite, or silicon carbide**

  **Acrylic paint or food coloring**

  **4K-inch (11cm) electric grinder (optional)**

  **Rubber mallet (optional)**

* You can also use 28 PCE (for "polymetric cone equivalent"), a lowduty firebrick, but the insulating firebrick (IFB) is easier to cut and will work just fine here.

  Position the electric kiln's steel stand in the desired location. If your kiln doesn't have a stand, use concrete blocks to support the bottom section. Don't stack the blocks tightly together; allow ¼ inch (6mm) air space between them. Never position a kiln directly on the floor of your studio. Doing so can cause a serious fire.

  Cut the two burner ports first. Rest the bottommost section of the kiln on a sturdy table, with one side of it hanging over the edge so you can access the bottom edge of the steel skin. Use the permanent marker and the tape measure to locate the center of the side of the faceted section, directly opposite the section that has the lid's hinge **(1)**.

**1** : Overhead view of kiln

  The inside edges of the ports should be positioned 16 inches (41cm) apart, so make two locator marks, each 8 inches (20cm) away from the center mark. Use your marker to register the edges of both burner ports. Draw the burner ports as two rectangles, each 4 inches (10cm) high by 6 inches (15cm) wide, at the bottom edge of the steel facing. Each rectangle will be 6 inches (15cm) wide and should start from the locator marks you just made **(2).**

**2** : Top view of burner ports

  Drill a hole, ½ inch (1.3cm) in diameter, in each of the upper corners of the two rectangles you've drawn. Use the tin snips to cut out the rectangle for each port. If steel skin is too tight, use the grinder to cut the skin. File any sharp edges and points. Put on the respirator. Using the top edges of the rectangular openings as guides, drill a series of perforating holes, ½ inch (1.3cm) apart, through the bricks.

  Now you'll cut up through the (undrilled) sides of the bricks with the saw. Make your cuts at an angle that widens out, so that the burners' flames can move unimpeded into the kiln.

  Break the bricks across the perforated top line; sometimes a chisel helps. Use the large file to smooth the three walls of the two burner ports. Position this bottom section of the kiln on the stand. Add the other sections, being sure to align the facets properly as you do.

  Stack concrete blocks, firebricks, or a combination of the two under each port opening, until the blocks are level with the openings' bottom edges. Now construct tunnel-like extensions, with two sidewalls and a spanner, for each of the port openings. These will be lined with cut pieces of K26 firebrick and supported by the stacks you just made. Cut the bricks to:

**Inside section:** 3 x 4 x 1 inches (7.5 x 10 x 2.5cm)

**Outside section:** 3 x 7 x 1 inches (7.5 x 18 x 2.5cm)

**Roof spanner:** 4½ x 6 x 1 inches (11 x 15 x 2.5cm)

The 4-inch (10cm) pieces line the ports' inside walls and the 7-inch (18cm) pieces insert into the outside walls. This creates a port that comes out of the kiln at a slight angle so the flames will run parallel to the trough inside **(3)**.

**3** : Burner port

  Mix the refractory mortar according to the manufacturer's directions. Use it to paste the port liner pieces to the kiln and to each other. Use the palette knife to apply the mortar to the brick and kiln face—but not the inner surfaces. When the bricks are in place, use more mortar to fill any gaps. You can also bind some ceramic fiber with mortar to secure the small structure even more firmly **(4)**.

**4** : Burner port showing cowl

  Cover the mortar and set it aside; you'll be using more of it later.

  Now you can stack the rest of the kiln sections back on top of each other. Make sure the facets line up as they did before you took the sections apart. Position the lid with the hinge on the side that is opposite the side with the burner ports.

  The next step is to construct a simple, L-shaped flue system, which includes an entry flue, trough, chimney flue, and chimney, out of K26 IFB **(5)**. The bricks in the kiln pictured here are a mix of 28 PCE firebricks—I used splits 1¼ inches (3.2cm) deep—and K23 IFB, cut to size, plus a few straights, which measure 9 x 4½ x 2½ inches (23 x 11 x 6cm). You have the option to use the full-sized straights for this flue system, but make sure the recommended interior measurements stay the same. It doesn't matter what the flue's outer dimensions are, though larger bricks may affect the amount of space between the burner ports.

**5** : Construct flue system

  Now you'll set bricks into a narrow channel across the kiln's floor. This channel will connect the entry flue to the chimney flue and let the exhaust gases travel under the pots and out the chimney. Arrange two brick walls between the pair of burner ports. Build the walls parallel to each other, standing the bricks on their narrower sides, 6½ inches (17cm) apart **(6)**. If the last bricks in each row come up short, fill the end gaps with IFB (insulated firebrick), and mortar them together. If the bricks are too tight, use the rubber mallet to place them. Each burner's flame will move along an outside wall of the trough.

**6** : Floor flue system (without shelf)

  Next, construct the entry flue at the end of the trough, against the wall that's below the lid's hinge **(7)**. The size of the flue box will be one brick's width, or 4½ inches (11cm), deep. The entry flue's final interior dimension will be 6½ inches (17cm) square. Cut each of the flue box's sidewalls 7½ inches (19cm) long. (When the kiln shelf covers the top of the trough, the flue's interior dimension will become the right size.) Stand one of the sidewalls on its end, on top of one of the trough rows, where it meets the wall. Make sure they are stable. Mortar the two sidewalls to the trough and the kiln's wall. Mortar a spanning brick that measures 9 x 4½ x 1½ inches (23 x 11 x 4cm) to the two sidewall bricks into place, for the roof of the flue box.

**7** : Collector flue

  Place a 20-inch (51cm) square shelf on top of the trough. Snug it up against the flue box you just made **(8)**.

**8** : Floor flue system (with shelf)

  The opening at the chimney end should measure at least 4½ x 6½ inches (11 x 17cm). The chimney rises from this end of the trough and exits through the lid, near the handle. The two parallel sides of the chimney are made from cut splits of firebrick that measure 9 x 3½ x 1½ inches (23 x 9 x 4cm). Stand them vertically and flush with the outer walls of the trough. Securely mortar them to the kiln wall and to the front-facing chimney bricks. Since the kiln's interior is curved, cut one edge of each split at a gentle angle so they'll fit well **(9)**.

**9** : Chimney and flue system (without shelf)

  The face of the chimney is also composed of splits 9 x 4½ x 1½ inches (23 x 11 x 4cm). These bricks are set horizontally, on one edge, all the way up. Securely mortar them to the inside face of the sidewall. The first facing brick spans right across the trough; mortar it into place. If your shelf is a bit long, cut notches in the sidewall bricks to get started and lay the first facing brick on top of the shelf, as shown in photo **10**. When positioned correctly, the two sidewalls and a face brick form a vertical channel with an interior measurement of 9 x 2½ inches (23 x 6cm).

**10** : Chimney flue stack mortared to the side wall

**11** : Chimney flue exit

**12** : Chimney and collection flue (note fiber gasket)

**GAS BURNERS FOR A CONVERTED KILN**

You're going to need two burners for this design. In order to get the right size burners, use the formula on this page to find the volume of the kiln, in cubic feet. Multiply the cubic feet by 10,000 British Thermal Units, or BTUs, and divide the result by 2 (the number of burners). The burners for a typical gas conversion kiln should be rated at 45,000 BTUs _each_. Have a licensed plumber install the gas line to the burner.

For a typical gas conversion kiln such as this one, you'll need the following gear for safe firing:

  **2 Venturi burners, 45,000 BTUs each, with pilot burners**

  **100-pound (45.5kg) propane tank**

  **2 gas regulators. One regulator must be located at the tank and the other within 15 feet (4.5m) of the kiln. Both regulators should be set at 5 psi.**

  **Black piping (it's always a good idea to have a licensed plumber do this work)**

  **One main gas shut-off valve, needle type**

  **One shut-off valve per burner, needle type**

  **High-pressure safety pilot valve with thermocouple**

Connecting and using this equipment still depends on your knowledge of safe mechanical practices. For more information, consult the latest version of the freely distributed International Fuel Gas Code for safety regulations and precautions. Don't take shortcuts when dealing with a gas appliance such as your kiln. If you can't locate your kiln in a protected outdoor setting—both electric and gas types—install a good ventilation system that expels all fumes from your work space.

To light your burners, see the sidebar on this page.

**common glaze types**

Glazes, and the innumerable variations possible when their basic formulations are adjusted, are often grouped according to their primary characteristics. This descriptive guide gives some examples taken from the rich and varied world of glaze types.

**Ash.** Oxides present in the ashes of burned wood create variegated colors and surfaces on fired clay. Wood ash glazes and patinas are usually dimpled with rivulets.

ASH

**Celadon.** Shiny, transparent glazes that are traditionally green, gray, blue, or amber. Their colors are derived from the presence of iron oxide in the recipe.

CELADON

**Chun.** A type of opalescent glaze that is usually light blue in color, with a soft-looking satin-gloss surface. Like celadon, chun glazes usually depend on iron for their coloration.

CHUN

**Copper red.** A reduction firing is needed to achieve the glossy, brilliantly red color.

COPPER RED

**Crystalline.** The formation of crystals that float in a glassy glaze usually develop when the melting glaze is low in viscosity. Recipes with titanium, zinc, or wollastonite tend to form crystals during firing.

CRYSTALLINE

**Majolica.** An opaque, tin- or zirconium-based type of pure-white glaze.

MAJOLICA

**Raku crackle.** This glaze requires a high-alkaline flux to help create its dynamic crackle effect.

RAKU

**Salt.** Adding sodium to the kiln chamber while firing unglazed clay bodies creates this dimpled "orange peel" surface.

SALT

**Shino.** Shino's naturalistic and varied tones come from the early melting of an abundant amount of sodium fired in a reduction atmosphere.

SHINO

**Tenmoku.** Varying percentages of iron create black, dark brown, or amber in this glossy glaze.

TENMOKU
**troubleshooting glaze flaws**

There are times when glazes don't perform exactly as we'd intended and we're left wondering what went wrong. It helps to keep in mind that materials change over time, applications can vary, the wall thickness of a pot can have a huge effect on glaze-body interface, and firing conditions present countless variables. To help you troubleshoot some specific common glaze problems, I've made a few suggestions below.

---

**FLAWS** | **POSSIBLE SOLUTIONS**

  | **Blistering.** Thin, fragile bubbles or craters in glazes containing certain ingredients. | • Check your notes for the length of time of the firing; may be the result of underfiring or overfiring.

• If the glaze recipe contains cornwall stone, manganese dioxide, soda ash, or lead, adjust the amounts.

  | **Crawling.** The glaze rolls back on itself, separating or beading up, and leaving patches or fissures of exposed clay. | • Apply a thinner coat of the glaze.

• Handle bisqueware with clean hands.

• Adjust the amount of clay, alumina, or zinc in the recipe.

• Glaze fire more slowly.

  | **Crazing.** A web-like series of super fine cracks in the glaze. | • Bisque fire to higher temperature.

• Fire more slowly during the last 100°F / 37.8°C.

• Increase the amount of silica in the formula.

  | **Pinholing.** Minute craters in the glaze surface | • More air needed during bisque firing.

• Fire more slowly at the peak of glaze firing.

• Reduce the amount of soda or potassium.

  | **Running.** Drips and rivulets in the glaze. | • May be the result of overfiring.

• Reduce the amount of flux in the glaze recipe.

• Apply the glaze more thinly.

  | **Shivering.** The glaze lifts, chips, or flakes off of the pot, most commonly along a sharp edge, rim, or lip; the opposite of the condition that causes crazing (see above). | • Add a fluxing agent, such as a feldspar, to the recipe.

**COLORANTS**

Colorants can be added to any base-type engobe recipe, but the percentage needed will vary according to its unique properties. Another way to color a base recipe is to use a manufactured fritted color, or a stain. Regardless, the amount of colorant—whether it's an oxide* or a stain—will vary; therefore, for the best results, always test the mixture with your own clay, kiln, and atmosphere.

• When zinc is in the unfired glaze coat, ***chrome's** color may be green to brown or pink. Also, high-calcium glazes can change the color to gray. Chrome is refractory. Use 0.5–6 percent.

• **Copper** carbonate and oxide create a range of greens in an oxidation atmosphere and reds in reduction—even in an engobe. Use 0.5–8 percent.

• ***Manganese** dioxide and manganese carbonate can create natural purple to chocolate brown, and even bronze, if used in high enough concentrations. If the manganese isn't ground finely enough, there will be speckling in the engobe. Use 0.5–12 percent.

• ***nickel** oxide can produce soft grays, and sometimes hints of green and blue, depending on the kiln's atmosphere and temperature, and how thick the glaze coat is. Nickel is refractory. Use 0.5–3 percent.

• **Rutile** is a form of titanium dioxide. It can create colors in the range of soft iron-yellow to burnt orange. Under or over certain glazes, rutile can go gray. Use 0.5–12 percent.

• ***Tin** oxide is an opacifier (i.e., it reduces a glaze's transparency). It can make an engobe white. Use 2–8 percent.

• ***Zirconium** is an opacifier, but is not as strong as the more expensive tin oxide. In an engobe, it makes a cooler white than tin does. Use 2–15 percent.

* Any oxide marked with an asterisk is known to be either a human health or an environmental hazard. Seek further information regarding how to protect yourself and safeguard both the local groundwater and/or the public water supply, before handling, firing, or eating from wares glazed with the material.

**glossary of ceramic terms**

**Absorbent.** The quality of a material to draw water into its structure through actions such as gravity or capillary. Green ware and bisque ware are most absorbent in the ceramic cycle, making them ideal for glazing.

**Appendage.** An object or a thing that is attached to a central form for aesthetic or utilitarian purposes. Appendages include spouts, handles, added feet, lids, and the like.

**Ash.** A material obtained by burning animal or vegetable material and composed of both organic and inorganic materials. When melted during a firing, the results of the interaction between the minerals may be seen in varied glaze effects.

**Atmosphere.** The condition, inside the kiln chamber, that is defined by the amount of oxygen or temperature present during firing.

**Atomizer.** A breath-operated device used for spraying small amounts of slip, engobe, or glaze onto a pot. By blowing air through a tube positioned over a draw pipe inserted into the liquid, the liquid is drawn up and out, creating a fine spray.

**Ball clay.** Highly plastic clay that is composed of fine particles and usually fires to a cream color because of the presence of iron and titanium.

**Bat.** A flat disk, usually made of wood, plaster, or plastic, that easily detaches from the wheel head; used to transport a pot without touching it.

**Batch.** A mixture of materials, in a quantity large enough to be used, that make a slip, engobe, clay body, or glaze.

**Bentonite.** A very plastic clay having super-fine particle sizes, originating from the decomposition of volcanic ash, and used in a glaze recipe to suspend the ingredients or else provide plasticity to a clay body.

**Bisque.** Either a) porous wares, strengthened by being fired to a low temperature or b) a necessary firing stage prior to the glazing process.

**Blistering.** Bubbles in fired glaze due to gases released by the clay or glaze during firing. Appears in the cooled ceramic piece if the bisque-fire temperature wasn't high or long enough, or if the glaze firing was done so quickly that the bubbles didn't have time to heal.

**Bloating.** Bubbles trapped inside the wall of a ceramic due to gases in the clay body not having been fully removed during the bisque firing, or else the kiln was fired too quickly at a low temperature during a glaze firing.

**Blunge.** Mixing water with clay or other materials to a usable consistency. Usually refers to the mixing of slips, engobes, or glazes with a mechanical impellor or auger.

**Body-glaze interface.** The point during melting when a clay body and glaze interact to the extent that there is bonding.

**Boiling point.** Because they become liquids at different melting points, the variable nature of a glaze's ingredients gives each glaze its own boiling point; for water, 212°F / 100°C.

**Bone china.** A translucent, porcelaneous ceramic invented in Britain. It derives its name from the inclusion of a high percentage of bone ash as flux.

**Bone dry.** A clay body, heated to just over 212°F / 100°C, without any atmospheric and physical moisture; bone-dry pots are completely dry and ready for firing.

**Boxing.** A space-efficient method for stacking pots, either lip to lip or foot ring to foot ring, for drying or firing.

**Casting slip.** A liquid form of clay suspended in water and used to create a clay form. Usually used in conjunction with a plaster mold.

**Catalyst.** Something that causes change in other more refractory materials, somewhat like a flux does, but doesn't undergo radical compounding change itself.

**Centering.** The term given to one of the first steps in making a symmetrical form on the potter's wheel. After the clay is secured to the wheel head, it is wetted and made to spin evenly and true before other stages of shaping.

**Ceramic.** A clay product permanently converted by firing.

**Chattering.** The rhythmic, bouncing motion of a tool's edge on a pot's surface during trimming; usually unintended, but may be used as a technique to create a decorative motif.

**Chemical water.** Water that is bound into the molecular structure of clay. It must be evaporated by firing to a minimum 1112°F / 600°C. When chemical water is gone, clay becomes ceramic. Chemical water makes up 14 percent, by weight, of dry clay.

**China.** Commonly used to refer to ceramics made from porcelain clay because of the association with that type of pottery's place of origin.

**China clay.** Another name for kaolin, and used regardless of where it's quarried; the main ingredient in porcelain clay bodies.

**Chuck.** A simple, thrown vessel made from stiff-moist clay, bisque-fired ceramic, or plaster; used to hold a form during a particular phase of throwing or trimming.

**Clay.** A malleable material made of hydrated silicate of alumina. Decomposed igneous rocks disintegrated by weathering and their movement by natural forces; classified as either primary or secondary, based on the distance transported from their source. The farther a clay has traveled the finer its particle sizes will be, resulting in greater plasticity.

**Clay body.** A compound mixture—made of natural clays, fluxes, and fillers—with dependable qualities; used to make forms that, when fired to specific temperatures and atmospheres, become durable ceramic objects.

**Compression.** A reduction in size as a result of pressure. In throwing, the method of making the clay tighter and less prone to cracking as it dries. In the relationship between a clay body and a glaze, proper compression makes the glaze fit the clay body well; too much compression, however, causes shivering.

**Coning.** A useful technique that, when used in the early stages of throwing, helps to center the clay. Also, the shape that results, as "cone."

**Cone pack.** One or more pyrometric cones set into a ceramic base and placed into the kiln to report the effects of temperature and changes to the rate at which the heat increases.

**Contraction.** A decrease in size due to temperature change. Because clay bodies and glazes contract after being fired, it's important that they do so easily.

**Cracking.** The effect of changes in thickness, form, shrinkage rate, and speed of drying on clay objects. Cracking in ceramic forms may be due to poor glaze fit, being bisque fired or cooled too fast, or when a reduction phase is begun too early, or too strongly.

**Crackle.** Small cracks caused by crazing of the matrix; sometimes used as a decorative effect.

**Crawling.** Glaze pooling or pulling away from the clay body, leaving bare spots. Sometimes used as a decorative element by deliberately formulating the glaze to ensure crawl.

**Crazing.** A network of fine cracks in the fired glaze, caused when the cooling glaze contracts more than the clay body does. Crazing can show up years after the firing took place. Unless the ware was under- or overfired, add 2-percent increments of silica when next mixing the glaze.

**Cross-draft kiln.** A kiln design that causes gases (flames) to enter the chamber at one wall and exit at the opposite wall, into the chimney.

**Damper.** Plate-like or other simple opening located in a kiln's chimney. It can be closed with bricks to reduce the amount of oxygen in the firing chamber. An active damper is slid open or closed, to regulate the flow of gases being emitted.

**De-airing.** Removing air pockets from pliable clay by hand or machine.

**Deflocculation.** To make a slip, engobe, or glaze more fluid by adding a soluble alkali.

**Double dipping.** Glazing by dipping a pot upside down, and then jerking the pot up while keeping the rim under the surface. The resulting splash inside the pot glazes its interior. Also, applying two or more layers of glazes to get a variable and blended effect.

**Dunting.** Unwanted cracks in a fired ceramic piece; caused by sudden temperature changes during firing or cooling.

**Earthenware.** Pots made with a clay having a porosity of 5 percent or greater; may also be used to refer to certain clay bodies or firing ranges.

**Engobe.** A clay slip with coloring oxides and flux added. Used as a decorative element or as a primary surface on a pot, and applied by brushing, dipping, or spraying.

**Expansion.** An increase in size caused by an increase in temperature.

**Feldspar.** A family of minerals formed in the earth from cooled and crystalized magma. Used primarily as fluxes in clay bodies and glazes; being composed of silica, alumina, and various alkalis makes feldspar a naturally occurring glaze.

**Fettling.** Using a fettling knife to remove clay from a form that is pliable to dry.

**Fireclay.** A family of plastic combinations of minerals formed from decomposed soils and vegetation; high in alumina content and therefore refractory.

**Firing.** The heating process by which clays and glazes are made ceramic; a minimum temperature of 1112°F / 600°C is required.

**Firing cycle.** The period of time over which clay pots are fired and cooled in a kiln to become ceramic.

**Fit.** The relationship between a clay body and glaze whereby they are able to expand and contract together sufficiently.

**Flocculation.** To make the heavier particles in a glaze, slip, or engobe suspend more readily by adding an acidic or a magnesium-based flocculant, such as epsom salt, to the mixture.

**Flux.** An alkaline oxide, or combination of oxides, that interacts with other oxides to cause melting to take place.

**Glaze.** A super-cooled liquid produced by fusing silica with soda, potash, and other oxides, including those such as alumina that assist in its adherence to and interface with clay. Sometimes called glost.

**Green ware.** A finished clay form that is not yet dry enough to be fired.

**Grog.** Ceramic particles, of various sizes, added to clay to improve its wet strength and other desirable throwing qualities like "tooth" (texture); usually made from high-fired fireclay or, less commonly, earthenware or porcelain.

**Heat-work.** The combined effects of time and temperature to which a ceramic is exposed within the kiln; measured by the pyrometric cone.

**High-fire glaze.** A glaze formulated to be fired at or above 2192°F / 1200°C.

**Impression.** A surface mark made by stamping or paddling a soft or leather-dry clay form.

**Inlay.** A decorative technique by which leather-dry clay is incised, then filled with a colored slip, engobe, or glaze; the excess is scraped off later, after drying. Also called mishima.

**Iron oxide.** The most common coloring agent used in clays and glazes. In combination with various other oxides, this metallic oxide produces browns, blacks, grays, greens, oranges, pinks, and yellows.

**Kaolin.** See China clay.

**Kiln.** The oven used to fire ceramics, usually constructed from refractory materials and designed according to the fuel needed.

**Kiln controller.** A digital machine, connected to thermo-couples and also to the power source of an electric kiln, that sends commands to a kiln's heating elements; used to operate complex firing cycles.

**Kiln furniture.** Refractory posts and shelves used to support pots inside a kiln during firing.

**Kiln sitter.** A mechanical device that assists in turning off an electric kiln at the end of a firing. Most kiln sitters feature a small rod that sits in the center of a cone that is suspended between two holders. When the given temperature is reached, the cone melts and the rod triggers the power to shut off.

**Kiln wash.** A thick, fluid mixture of refractory materials applied to kiln shelves and furniture to protect from glaze drips and adhesion.

**Kneading.** Stretching and compressing clay to remove air bubbles and make it ready for handling.

**leather-dry.** Clay that is no longer tacky and is nearly stiff; may be trimmed, cut, assembled, or carved.

**low-fire temperature.** A range of temperatures to which certain clay bodies and glazes are fired; from cone 022 (1085°F / 585°C) to cone 2 (2057°F / 1125°C).

**Marbling.** The effect of insufficient kneading.

**Matte.** The surface quality of a glaze that is soft, usually opaque, and nonreflective.

**Maturing temperature.** The temperature to which a glaze or clay body is fired to attain either a full melt or vitrification.

**Melting point.** The temperature at which a raw mineral oxide or a mixture of oxides begins to melt.

**Mesh.** See Sieve.

**Mid-range.** Temperatures to which certain clay bodies and glazes are fired; from cone 3 (2093°F / 1145°C) to cone 7 (2191°F / 1200°C).

**Motif.** A shape or an image within a pattern or alone, as decoration.

**Mullite.** An alumina silicate in a clay body produced by vitrification. Because of its large crystal structure, this strong material is often used in the manufacture of kiln furniture.

**Neutral atmosphere.** The condition inside a kiln that is being fired somewhere between a complete reduction and a complete oxidation atmosphere.

**On-glaze colorant.** A wash comprised of one or more oxides that is used to paint decoration on top of a glazed surface before firing.

**Opacifier.** A mineral oxide, such as tin oxide and zirconium, that causes clouding of a glaze. Also, oxides that in excess cause crystalline or bubbling matrices are such agents.

**Oven ware.** A family of pottery forms that is able to withstand extreme changes in temperatures. Made from ceramics that are either porous but fragile, or vitrified to the extent that the free silica has been sufficiently melted to become fused; making successful ovenware provides a difficult challenge for the potter.

**Oxidation.** Often referring to the atmosphere in a kiln, it is technically the combining of oxygen with compounds found in a ceramic, at temperatures above red heat. Oxidation wields a different effect on clay bodies and glazes than neutral or reduction atmospheres do. Electric kilns are the most effective tools for achieving oxidation atmospheres because of the absence of gases introduced by carbonaceous fuels.

**Paddle.** A tool used to make impressions into, change the form of, or compress a pliable clay surface or wall.

**Peephole.** A small opening in a kiln's wall.

**Physical water.** H20. Water that has been added to a clay body during its manufacture; it is removed by evaporation.

**Pinhole.** Tiny craters or indents in the surface of a glaze after it has been melted.

**Plaster.** Semihydrated calcium sulphate made from gypsum; used for making molds, stamps, and drying slabs because it absorbs moisture from and releases clay easily.

**Plasticity.** The ability of pliable clay to be easily given form and either maintain that form or by force be changed instantly; a phenomenon by which a nonelastic solid is at the same time a liquid.

**Porcelain.** A type of clay body or ceramic. Usually white and translucent, with a post-fired absorption rate of 0 to 1 percent.

**Porosity.** The quality of a fired ceramic to absorb moisture through capillary action.

**Preheating.** Initial firing step that evaporates physical water from clay bodies and glazes.

**Primary clay.** Any type of clay found at its source of origin; kaolin and bentonite are two.

**Pugmill.** A machine that mixes and compresses a malleable clay body, thereby removing air pockets; a machine that uses the process of vacuum to do this.

**Pull.** Raising a pot's wall during throwing or making a handle; also, the phenomenon of gases being drawn up a kiln's chimney.

**Pyrometer.** An instrument used to indicate the temperature inside a kiln. The pyrometer measures the reading coming from a thermocouple or probe.

**Pyrometric cone.** An instrument, made from a combination of clay and glaze materials, that responds to the amount of heat-work happening inside a kiln during firing.

**Quartz.** Another name for silica, flint, and Si02; the primary form of silica.

**Raku.** The process of firing a ceramic that originated in Japan. This fast firing technique requires that the clay body be formulated so that dunting is unlikely because the ceramic is withdrawn from the kiln usually at temperatures around 1940°F / 1060°C. Oftentimes a heavy reduction done in organic materials is a final feature of the technique.

**Re-absorption.** The action by which a dry clay body draws moisture from the air.

**Reclaim.** To process and make useful a clay body after it has dried.

**Reduction.** The condition of the atmosphere inside a kiln when oxygen is removed from the oxides in the ceramics.

**Refractory.** Resistant to high temperatures; brick, ceramic fiber (blanket), and other products manufactured using materials with high melt points.

**Resist.** A material or technique for blocking areas of clay from the adherence of an engobe, slip, or glaze.

**Rib.** A broad, flat tool, made from wood, ceramic, metal, plastic, or rubber, used to shape or compress a clay body; shapes and sizes vary greatly.

**Run.** When glaze or ceramic color moves as a result of melt and gravity.

**Sand.** Silica, or quartz, found in nature in a granular form. While most sands contain other oxides as well, silica sand is a pure form that features a high melting point.

**Satin matte.** The surface quality of a glaze that looks waxy soft and at least somewhat opaque.

**Scoring.** To scratch or incise a clay surface onto which an appendage is to be added or attached.

**Scumming.** Blemishes on the surface of bisque ware or other porous ceramics caused by the migration of alkalis.

**Secondary clay.** Sedimentary clay that has been removed by natural forces from its point of origin.

**Sedimentation.** The settling of heavier minerals out of a solution.

**Setters.** Kiln furniture designed to hold tiles or pots in a stack, thus saving space.

**Sgrafitto.** From the Italian; incising through a layer or layers of slip or engobe to expose the layer underneath it.

**Shard.** A broken piece of ceramic, glaze, or glass.

**Shivering.** The flaking of glaze from the surface of a ceramic. Considered a glaze defect, shivering occurs because the clay shrinks or contracts more than the glaze does, placing it under a too high compression.

**Short.** A term describing a clay body having too little plasticity and subsequently slumping or cracking easily.

**Shrinkage.** Decrease in size due to the evaporation of physical and chemical waters as well as melt during firing.

**Sieve.** A tool used to screen larger particles from slips, engobes, and glazes.

**Silica.** One of the primary oxides in clays, glazes, engobes, and refractory materials.

**Sinter.** To bond together refractory materials without melting them. Sintering is the stage before melt.

**Slake.** Rehydrating dry, unfired clay by shattering and then dissolving it in water.

**Slip.** Clay or clay body mixed with water to a thick consistency.

**Slip-glaze.** A glaze made up of 50 percent or more clay.

**Slurry.** A thick, creamy suspension of clay in water.

**Soap.** A refractory brick used as kiln furniture or construction that usually measures 9 x 2½ x 2¼ inches (23 x 6 x 5.5cm).

**Split.** A refractory brick used in kiln construction; usually 9 x 4½ x 1¼ inches (23 x 11 x 3cm).

**Stilt.** A refractory support to hold or suspend pots slightly above the kiln shelf during firing.

**Stoneware.** A mid-range to high-temperature type of clay; fires between cone 6 to cone 10.

**Straight.** A refractory brick used in kiln construction; usually 9 x 4½ x 2½ inches (23 x 11 x 6cm).

**Terra-cotta.** Italian word for fired earth. Often used to describe low-temperature orange to red earthenware clay bodies or ceramics.

**Terra sigillata.** A suspension of water, fine particle clay, and sometimes coloring oxides, that is brushed, dipped, or sprayed onto a claywork. When burnished, terra sigillata has a shiny or waxy surface that, because it is tightly compressed, helps prevent the absorption of water.

**Thermal shock.** Cracking caused by stress within a ceramic object due to a sudden change in temperature or because a glaze did not expand as much as the pot did.

**Thermocouple.** A metal probe capable of withstanding high temperatures that is positioned inside a kiln. It relays energy to a pyrometer, which displays the result.

**Throwing.** Using a turning wheel to shape clay.

**Tooth.** The word used to describe a quality of coarseness in a clay body. Tooth is created by the addition of aggregates such as grog or sand to the body.

**Translucent.** The quality of a melted glaze in which there is some scattering of light; not completely transparent.

**Transparent.** A melted glaze in which light can fully penetrate the glass matrix.

**Trimming.** To remove excess or support clay from a leather-dry form with a tool.

**Turning.** See Trimming.

**Undercut.** A bevel, cut into the base of a freshly thrown pot, that makes removing and trimming a pot easier.

**Underfired.** A term describing a ceramic that was not fired to the maturing temperature intended. Underfiring can cause defects such as too much porosity, glaze crazing, pinholing, dullness, lighter color than intended, weakness, or fragility.

**Underglaze.** A decorative, glaze-like material that is applied to either a clay body or a ceramic; it bonds to the ceramic to nearly the same extent that a glaze does. Most intense effect when coated by a transparent glaze.

**Vitrification.** The reaction of a ceramic, when exposed to a maturing temperature, to melt but still hold its shape.

**Wedging.** A clay preparation technique that combines mixing with compression by hand.

**Wheel.** Potter's wheel. A machine driven by electric motor or foot that provides the torque and centrifugal force necessary for throwing, trimming, or decorating clay shapes. Egyptian potters are credited for the invention of the potter's wheel.

# AUTHOR'S NOTE

The primary action of this book concerns the status of the Low Countries—today, Belgium and the Netherlands—during the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. As Europe emerged from its feudal past, this territory came under the sovereignty of Habsburg Spain, which had extensive holdings across the Continent. Spanish rule in the Low Countries was so divisive as to instigate a prolonged war of rebellion—the Eighty Years' War—within the seventeen provinces of the greater Netherlands. The ten southern provinces (modern Belgium) remained loyal to Spain, and came to be known as the Spanish Netherlands, or Flanders. The seven northern provinces fought for their independence, and became the Dutch nation, commonly known as Holland. This conflict ensnared all the great powers of western Europe, who were perpetually jockeying among themselves in disputes of political ambition, commerce, religion, and territory.

For the sake of clarity, I generally use the designation "Flanders" to refer to the southern, loyalist region that is properly known as the Spanish Netherlands. In fact, Flanders was just one of several provinces that constituted the Spanish Netherlands. Similarly, I use the designation "Holland" to refer to the rebellious Dutch provinces to the north, though it was just one of several provinces in the coalition that became the modern Netherlands. It was standard practice to refer to "Flanders" and "Holland" (and "Fleming" and "Hollander") at the time the book is set, so it is reasonable to turn to them again here. The Latin term _Belgica_ , also familiar during that period, referred to the Low Countries in their entirety.

For convenience, dates are regularized to the Continental standard calendar. England, at the time, operated on a calendar ten days behind the rest of Europe, with the New Year begun on the twenty-fifth of March. There was also no standard currency used across Europe during this period. For reference, one Flemish guilder or florin was roughly equivalent to one-tenth of an English pound and a twelfth of a Continental crown. An average annual salary for an unskilled tradesman in Flanders was roughly 300 guilders.

# PROLOGUE

Few artists have left so deep an imprint on their times as Peter Paul Rubens, the painter whose sense of grandiosity and drama gave visual definition to Baroque power. Fusing the lessons of the Italian Renaissance and the artistic traditions of his native Flanders, Rubens created a style that was entirely original and universally appealing, an international language that bespoke authority and cultivation. It was a heroic vision, one that allowed him to picture the most powerful men and women of his day, and the institutions they controlled, not necessarily as they were, but as they wished to be seen. His unique ability and keen sense of entrepreneurship brought him a seemingly endless stream of royal clients, but he was adored by the general public as well, especially for the moving evocations of devotion he created for their places of worship. No artist better managed the delicate task of translating the ethereal passion and splendor of religious faith onto canvas. The reverence shown him by other artists was almost fanatic. A young Rembrandt, like many painters who followed in his wake, modeled himself on Rubens—he even dressed in imitation of the great master from Antwerp.

The nearly universal esteem in which Rubens was held, combined with his access to the highest reaches of international power, provided the foundation for his conscription into diplomatic service. Painting gave Rubens the perfect cover for clandestine work; he could appear at any foreign court and always use his art to allay suspicion of ulterior motives. It's hard to imagine this happening in our own time; we don't expect artists to be spies or diplomats. Political figures dabbling in art is one thing—Churchill and Eisenhower were amateur painters, and Hitler a failed professional—but not the reverse. From the Romantic era, we have inherited a vision of the painter as an emotionally volatile, impecunious radical: a critic or enemy of the state, and not someone to be entrusted with its most delicate and urgent business.

Rubens does not fit into that archetype. He was born in 1577 and came of age at a time when painting was still a respected guild profession. Those who met him almost invariably remarked on his affable nature and winning personality. He was tall and physically attractive, with a disarming, scholarly mien. His innate charisma was only augmented by his preternatural artistic ability and his encyclopedic knowledge of subjects ranging from architecture to political theory to zoology. The images for which he is now most famous—swooning women, their flesh alive in puckered ecstasy—suggest a man of unchecked libertinism. In fact, he was a devoted husband and generally moderate in his personal appetites, the chief exception being his zeal for work. A life so disciplined and successful might well have transformed him into an insufferable pedant, but instead he wore his authority lightly, and that only magnified it. He had few vices besides the occasional flash of pride.

What prompted Rubens's engagement in politics was the condition of his native Flanders, a land beset by sectarian violence and occupied by a negligent foreign empire, Spain, to which he owed allegiance. His beloved but decimated Antwerp, once a haven of international trade and culture, sat on the front lines of a war of independence waged against that Spanish empire by the nascent Dutch republic to the north. Rubens made it his personal mission to resolve that seemingly intractable conflict, known to history as the Eighty Years' War. It was a goal he pursued with the same energy that he brought to his art, and one for which he risked all that he had acquired—his career, his reputation, his life.

This project, more ambitious than any painting, consumed him for over a decade, during which time he traveled from capital to capital, often under false pretenses, to negotiate with statesmen and monarchs who were also clients. Sequestered in their luxurious palaces, isolated from their subjects and the world beyond by meticulously orchestrated systems of protocol and social stratification, these rulers could be oblivious to and sometimes contemptuous of political realities. Decisions of enormous consequence were often made on ideological grounds, for the sake of national or personal pride, or merely on whim. Rubens, in contrast, was a consistent voice of moderation, a pragmatist or _politique_ , in the parlance of the day.

Sectarian conflict and political dogmatism still plague the community of nations, a reality that gives particular resonance to the story of a moderate and pragmatic man who spent so much of his life fighting entrenched forces in the halls of international power. For all its relevance, however, Rubens's diplomatic work and philosophy are for the most part unknown but to scholars, an unfortunate, though not surprising, circumstance. Contemporary audiences can hardly be expected to recall his political career when even his accomplishments as a painter remain largely unfamiliar. Among the great masters of art history, Rubens is something of a forgotten man, respected but misunderstood, hidden in plain sight. The reasons are many. There is no single painting that defines his career, no image so iconic as the _Mona Lisa_ or the _Demoiselles d'Avignon_. He does not conform to our favored image of the artist as a tortured soul. The allegorical, mythological, and biblical figures that populate his canvases are alien to modern viewers, and those canvases can be so large and so complicated as to defy ready explanation. He has been tarred by the undistinguished politics of his clients. To many, he is simply the man who painted lascivious pictures of fat, naked women.

Our inability to fully grasp Rubens's achievement is at least in part a failure of narrative. His story and his paintings have been robbed of their urgency over the centuries following his death. What passed for common knowledge and experience in the seventeenth century can seem altogether foreign to a modern audience. It is the historian's challenge to bridge this divide, and the rewards are well worth the effort. Rubens was possessed of an alchemical gift, an ability to bring colorful, breathtaking life to inanimate matter, and he is responsible for some of our most arrestingly beautiful and emotionally stirring investigations of the human condition. The essential lessons of these works are as fresh now as they were four hundred years ago, and we can recapture them in all their complex grandeur if we give the Rubens story the careful and sustained attention it so richly deserves.

# CHAPTER I  
A NOVICE WITHOUT EXPERIENCE

You are going as official representative into Spain, a country different in her ways and customs from Italy and unknown to you. Furthermore, it is your first commission. Hence if you make a good showing in this office, as everybody hopes and believes, you will gain high honor; and so much higher, the greater the difficulties.

—NICCOLÒ MACHIAVELLI

Sometime in the late spring of 1602—there is no record of exactly when—Vincenzo Gonzaga, the Duke of Mantua, decided it would be a good idea to send an extremely large gift to Philip III, the king of Spain. This was to be an act of considerable generosity, but not one motivated by pure altruism. To be a minor European monarch in the seventeenth century was to live in fear of Spain's pitiless and well-disciplined _tercios_. Those professional armies, bristling with artillery, pikes, and Toledo steel, and drilled in formations that seemed well-nigh invincible, made Spain the most potent military force on the Continent. Spain's possessions encompassed much of Italy, including Lombardy, Mantua's neighbor to the west. Vincenzo, no fool, eyed Spanish power with a healthy wariness. Like Philip, he was of Habsburg blood, but attachment to Europe's foremost dynasty did not guarantee the autonomy of his duchy. It was therefore only prudent that Vincenzo place himself squarely within Philip's good graces, as the young king was new to his throne.

Philip had a reputation as something of a sportsman, so Vincenzo tailored his offering accordingly. The centerpiece of the gift was to be a plush riding carriage driven by six of the finest horses from the duke's stable, revered across Europe for its thoroughbreds. That was a good start, and Vincenzo added to it with eleven harquebus guns decorated with whalebone and silver filigree, a rock crystal vase filled with perfume, and—somewhat immodestly—portraits of himself and his wife for the king's cabinet. These items were for Philip alone, but the duke did not stop there, for he knew that the king, in his hedonistic youth, had voluntarily surrendered much of his authority to his rapacious political Svengali, Francisco Gómez de Sandoval y Rojas, the Duke of Lerma. He, too, would be on the receiving end of Vincenzo's generosity.

Whereas Philip was a Habsburg scion, Lerma was born to minor nobility, and only created a duke by an act of his patron, the king. As with so many of history's arrivistes, Lerma understood the practice of collecting art, traditionally a pastime of royalty, to be a path to improved social respectability. Vincenzo's gift to him, then, was shrewdly designed to appeal to a man who would be a great connoisseur from a man who could already claim that distinction: some twenty old-master paintings, most of them actually copies of works by Raphael, several of which belonged to Vincenzo himself. (In an era before the easy mechanical reproduction of color images, there was little stigma attached to well-executed copies, even if originals were preferred and more valuable.) Lerma's own favorite minister, or _valido_ , the ruthless Don Rodrigo Calderón, would also receive works copied from the Mantuan collection, along with damask and cloth of gold. Lerma's religious sister would have a crystal crucifix and a pair of candelabra. A cash gift would be provided to the director of music at the royal chapel—Vincenzo was a patron of that art as well.

That Vincenzo might deliver these gifts himself was out of the question; that would have been too great an act of fealty for someone of his stature. The duke was a prideful man—in his own youth he had even killed a man over a minor indiscretion—and considerably older than Philip, who was still in his early twenties. Vincenzo thus preferred to cast himself as a benevolent elder statesman, an avuncular figure to be respected as a fellow Habsburg sovereign. He had even taken to the battlefield on behalf of the Habsburg cause, participating in a series of campaigns against the Ottomans, usually to his discredit. (He was an early—and failed—experimenter with poison gas; inept soldiering was something of a Gonzaga family tradition.) With this in mind, Vincenzo decided that an emissary would chaperone the gift. Any number of courtiers might have qualified for this job. The duke, like so many royals, surrounded himself with a cadre of ambitious grandees who would have thrilled at the prospect of a trip to the great Spanish court, not to mention a personal audience with Philip, the highest of royal highnesses. Vincenzo, however, did not choose any of these men. Instead, the duke summoned into his chamber a young Flemish painter with neither noble blood nor diplomatic pedigree. Vincenzo required someone reliable, preferably a painter who could handle any minor restoration work necessary after the long trip across the Mediterranean. But this agent also had to be someone with a bit of panache: someone who could handle the inevitable obstacles of a long journey while keeping its purpose quiet, for the duke most assuredly did not want every royal on the Italian boot to know of his private business groveling before the Spanish throne. More important, however, Vincenzo required someone who could represent him with appropriate dignity before his Habsburg relation in Madrid.

PETER PAUL RUBENS, age twenty-five, had been on the duke's payroll for only two years when he was selected for this mission. In that time, he had worked without ceremony on tasks of no great import: the minor portraits and copy work that were the routine business of a court studio. There was something about Rubens, though, that made him stand out from the several other painters employed by Vincenzo. People were naturally drawn to him, and the duke in particular. Vincenzo may even have noticed a slight resemblance between himself and the artist fifteen years his junior, even if the younger man, to be frank, had a good deal more hair and a good deal less paunch around the middle. Rubens was unquestionably handsome: tall for the age, with gently receding brown hair, neatly trimmed whiskers, and a piercing gaze. Those who knew him found him to be confident but not cocky, with an innate charisma that attracted both sexes. He possessed that ineffable quality Italians called _sprezzatura_ —a kind of easy, knowing charm. In the brief time they spent together, Rubens managed to impress Vincenzo as a quick-witted, refined, and highly intelligent individual of no small ambition. He was comfortable in the society of court, obsequious when circumstances demanded, and possessed of a diplomat's natural ability to appear both deferential and sincere even when conveying unpleasant information or shaving the rough edges of truth. That he was gifted with languages was especially useful; already he was fluent in Dutch, French, German, Italian, Latin, and Spanish.

Despite these qualities, Rubens was an unorthodox candidate for an important embassy. Diplomatic work was typically reserved for members of the aristocracy, men with political experience and the means to fund the considerable expenses of a life at court. Only those of high breeding, it was thought, could be expected to have the social dexterity and intellectual aptitude necessary to represent a sovereign prince in a foreign land. There were, however, exceptions to this rule. In one of the earliest primers on ambassadorial conduct, the Dutch-born diplomat Abraham de Wicquefort wrote that "it be not absolutely necessary, that the Embassador should be a Man of Birth, yet at the same time there must be nothing sordid nor mean in him."

As members of the court, painters were granted a standing above that of other tradesmen, and could be counted on to possess a worldliness typically restricted to those of hereditary advantage. Indeed, the profession required mastery of a broad range of fields, from chemistry (required to mix pigments), geometry (for perspective), and anatomy (for the drawing of the figure) to the classical and biblical history that served as the subject matter of so much painting. The most celebrated artists, prized for their seemingly magical image-making prowess, on occasion became trusted princely advisers. Leonardo da Vinci was a counselor to several princes (often on matters of defense and engineering) and in his later years an intimate of the French king François I. Jan van Eyck, until Rubens the most famous of Flemish painters, represented the duke of Burgundy on several diplomatic missions. Gentile Bellini, in 1457, was dispatched by the Venetian senate as a goodwill emissary to the Ottoman sultan Mehmet II at Constantinople. At the time of his trip, Rubens had yet to achieve the artistic reputation of Bellini, but his presence would similarly confer a bit of the Gonzaga family's considerable cultural authority on the Spanish court. That the paintings sent with him were largely copies of works from the Mantuan collection, rather than originals, only reinforced the sense of paternalism that Vincenzo hoped to convey. Every time the king and the duke glanced at these works, they would be reminded of both the magnificence and the munificence of their esteemed Mantuan ally.

The choice of an artist, then, was not unprecedented, but the choice of this artist, Rubens, occasioned a good deal of chatter among Vincenzo's notoriously chippy courtiers. He had good manners, yes, but he was not of aristocratic blood, and he was not a member of Vincenzo's inner circle—for that matter, _he wasn't even Italian_. His relevant experience was, indeed, practically nonexistent, though he had been prepared, at least in his early years, for a life in court service. As a child, he had been enrolled, along with his older brother Philip, in Rombout Verdonck's school for boys, the academy of choice for Antwerp's burgher elite. There, the Rubens brothers were drilled in the classics: Virgil, Horace, Pliny, and especially Seneca, whose stoicism was considered a philosophical model for contemporary behavior. Art was not on the program. Jan Rubens, the boys' late father, had been a lawyer and an alderman, and it seemed the young Peter Paul was headed down a similar path. He had always been an eager student, and a gifted one. The painter's nephew would later write that "he learned with such facility that he easily outstripped his classmates." Economic circumstances, however, put an end to Rubens's formal schooling at the age of thirteen. In 1590, the family education fund was diverted to provide a dowry for an older sister, Blandina. Rubens's evident intelligence and charm, even then, made him a prime candidate for a career as a court functionary, and his devoted mother, Maria, arranged through family connections to have him set up as a page in the residence of the Countess Marguerite de Ligne-Arenberg, whose father-in-law had been a governor-general of the Netherlands during the reign of Philip II.

It was a good appointment, but Rubens was unhappy. "There always glimmered inside him a desire for the noble art of painting," wrote Joachim von Sandrart, a German painter who traveled with Rubens in his later years. As a child, he had spent hour after hour poring over the woodblock prints of the artists Hans Holbein and Tobias Stimmer, which were popular among middle-class families like the Rubenses. Young Peter Paul was a natural with a pen, and found himself especially drawn to the robust figures in Stimmer's book of illustrated stories from the Bible, which had a physical presence so strong—like the imposing statues of cathedral facades—that it seemed they might just stomp off the page. From even those early drawings it was plainly evident that Rubens had artistic talent, and now he wanted to make a career of it. This was not an unprecedented decision for a Rubens; an older brother, Jan Baptist, had left the family many years earlier to pursue a career in the arts, and was thought to be in France. Rubens was not prepared to forsake his kin as his sibling had, but life as a functionary was not going to satisfy him either.

Whether or not she approved, Maria understood that once her headstrong young son had fixated on some goal, refusing him would be pointless. Again using family connections, he was apprenticed to Tobias Verhaecht, an Antwerp landscape painter of minor reputation who was a distant relative by marriage. Roughly a year later he moved on to the atelier of Adam van Noort, a respected member of the painters' guild, and some two years after that to the studio of Otto van Veen, who figured among Antwerp's artistic elite. He learned the basics of his craft in these apprenticeships: how to make pigments and prime a canvas, the techniques required of different mediums, how to layer colors, how to model a figure, how to compose the elements of an image. Soon enough he was working on canvases that would be finished by his masters. His education was more than just practical. Van Veen especially encouraged Rubens's academic interests. Before establishing his studio, Van Veen had traveled through Italy, where he absorbed the ideals of the Renaissance and the classical tradition. This was not uncommon at the time. Among the informal circle of like-minded humanists who dominated Antwerp culture, an extended tour of Italy was practically de rigueur. Even Jan Rubens, the painter's father, had made such a trip, earning his law degree in Rome after seven years of study abroad. Van Veen was more of a proselytizer than most. Upon his return he went so far as to assume a Romanized name: Octavius Vaenius.

By 1598, Rubens had completed his training and become a member in good standing of the Guild of Saint Luke, the painters' guild. He was a master, but he knew that he did not have all of the education he required, and he could see this deficiency quite plainly in his first commissions. A large panel painting of Adam and Eve showed his promise, but there was an undeniable stiffness to the picture, a frozen quality, that he intuitively understood as a weakness. Italy beckoned.

Rubens's quest to travel abroad for personal and professional enrichment was contingent upon his receipt of documents from the Antwerp town hall. These letters were required of all travelers, and verified that their bearers had good standing in the community and clean health—"no plague or contagious disease." Rubens received his papers on May 8, 1600. The next day he was off, accompanied by his first pupil, Deodate del Monte, who was similarly certified and would serve as a faithful assistant for many years to come. They traveled by horse, and though there is no precise record of their path, in all likelihood they traveled south and west, crossing through Alpine passes into northern Italy. Their first destination was Venice, a city that had supplanted Rome as an artistic capital for a brief moment in the previous century. If Venice had lost that momentum, it could nevertheless boast a modern school of painting that was like nothing Rubens had seen in Antwerp. In place of the studied classicism of Van Veen, the works of Bassano, Veronese, Tintoretto, and above all Titian, with their explosive colors, dynamic compositions, and expressive brushwork, suggested new directions for the young painter.

Rubens made it to Venice in time for the city's June carnival, a raucous annual event of masquerades, feasts, exhibitions, and performances with a history dating back to the thirteenth century. Vincenzo was also in town for the festivities, as an honored guest. The duke was a man of considerable appetites and liked to be on hand when there was a good debauch to be had—he was notoriously ill-tempered when not sated. To prevent this eventuality, the duke traveled with a sizable entourage, a group that included his secretary and chief political officer, Annibale Chieppio, a chubby-cheeked Milanese with a punctilious nature. In addition to his diplomatic duties, Chieppio kept an eye peeled for fresh artistic talent for the duke's Mantuan studio. At some point during the carnival, he met the enterprising young master from Antwerp. A review of the work Rubens had brought with him over the Alps was apparently enough to convince Chieppio to add him to the Mantuan payroll. Vincenzo already had one Flemish painter on staff, the portraitist Frans Pourbus, and that had worked out well. If nothing else, Rubens would prove useful in filling out Vincenzo's nascent "Gallery of Beauties." The duke enjoyed the prestige of his art collection, but he was frankly more interested in the lascivious pleasures it might provide him, and kept his court studio busy knocking out portraits of Europe's most attractive ladies. Rubens would soon find that work beneath his dignity, but for the moment he was happy for the appointment, which came with a respectable salary and accommodations in the royal compound. That same October, when Vincenzo left Mantua for Florence to attend the proxy marriage of Marie de' Medici to King Henry IV of France, Rubens was brought along as part of the duke's retinue.

That wedding, which united the Medici and Capetian dynasties, gave Rubens a taste of royal splendor that made a lasting impression. The ceremony took place at the Basilica di Santa Maria del Fiore, under the soaring vault of Brunelleschi's great dome. At the sumptuous banquet that followed, figures dressed as Roman gods serenaded dignitaries assembled from across Europe. (Henry, however, awaited his bride back in France, not wanting to expose himself to the predations of his prospective relatives.) In the future, Marie would become one of Rubens's most important patrons and political allies, but at her nuptial event he was relegated to the periphery. It served, however, as a useful lesson in the formalities and grand scale of Baroque political theater.

Rubens completed his first formal diplomatic "mission" for Vincenzo in the following year, 1601, when he delivered a letter from the duke to Alessandro Cardinal Montalto, nephew and adviser to Pope Sixtus V. The job, not a particularly difficult one, required the navigation of the halls of Roman power, but served primarily as an excuse to send Rubens to Rome, where he stayed for eight months making copies of old-master works for the duke. He also took on private commissions during his residency in the Eternal City, in the process substantially elevating his reputation as an artist.

That budding notoriety may well have been a factor when Vincenzo made the decision to send Rubens abroad in 1602. Word that Rubens was a bright new talent was already beginning to filter through Europe's capitals, and the fact that Vincenzo could claim him as a member of his artistic stable would be seen as yet another feather in the duke's cap. As an added bonus, Rubens could paint all the most attractive women in Madrid for Vincenzo's cabinet. Indeed, the painter would be instructed to return from Madrid by way of Paris for no other reason than to bring images of the fairest figures in that city back for the duke's museum of high-end soft-core pornography.

Vincenzo, then, knew just what he was doing when he had Rubens summoned to his private apartments at the Castello di San Giorgio. The artist walked briskly, as was his wont, through the halls of the palace and was ushered into the duke's presence by an elaborately uniformed chamberlain. Chieppio was there to provide him with his instructions, or at least the basics; there'd be plenty of time to go over logistics before his departure.

It was a plum assignment, and Rubens knew it. His whole Italian experience had thus far eclipsed all of his aspirations. He had departed Antwerp in an effort to enrich himself intellectually, and almost at once he had found himself attached to one of the most distinguished courts south of the Alps. The tasks of the Mantuan studio had proven to be no great challenge for him, and he had virtually unlimited access to the duke's collection of old masters, which he could study at his leisure. He had already traveled to Florence and to Rome on the duke's payroll, and now he was being offered the opportunity to ingratiate himself with the new Spanish king and his many acolytes, all potential clients. The logistical and diplomatic demands of the trip would be a chore and a distraction from Rubens's primary passion—his art—but the benefits were so great as to outweigh any thought of refusal. At the very least, he would have access to the famed royal collections in Madrid and at the Escorial, the art-filled monastery and palace complex in the nearby Guadarrama hills. And so when the delicate final moments of his meeting with Vincenzo and Chieppio arrived, Rubens was effusive. Yes, he was very pleased to be charged with this mission, and he would do all in his power to represent the duke with appropriate dignity.

IT WAS NEARLY a year before Rubens actually left Mantua with Vincenzo's gifts for the Spanish king and his courtiers. That long delay, the product of some bureaucratic snafu, augured poorly for the journey. At least it should have given the palace stewards time enough to map out an easy route to Spain for the painter, one that would have avoided mountain passes, unfriendly tax collectors, and the prying eyes of the duke's rivals. Unfortunately, careful attention was not devoted to the logistics of the journey, and Rubens did not have the experience to see just what trouble lay in store for him.

All this was beginning to dawn on him, however, when he found himself standing uncomfortably in an opulent Pisan receiving room before Vincenzo's uncle Ferdinand I de' Medici, the Grand Duke of Tuscany. This was in late March 1603, when he was already three weeks into his long-delayed journey. Rubens recognized Ferdinand's shrewd countenance; he had seen him in person a few years earlier, at the proxy wedding of Henry IV and Marie de' Medici in Florence. But that viewing was from a distance only. This audience was something altogether more intimate, and Rubens was grateful that Ferdinand opened it with a disarmingly friendly introduction. The grand duke politely inquired as to the painter's background and his purpose in Pisa, a long distance and a difficult mountain passage from his patron's Mantuan palace. Rubens offered the truth, though he went light on the details of his mission; he was in no position to discuss Vincenzo's affairs with another prince, no matter their relation. The grand duke nodded. In fact, the question was a con. He knew precisely who Rubens was, where he was going, why he was going there, and what he was carrying along with him. To demonstrate this knowledge, he cut Rubens off in midstream and proceeded, in rather bemused fashion, to rattle off the entire extravagant catalog headed for Philip III—every last item, down to the final whalebone harquebus. It was an impressive performance, and it concluded with the grand duke "asking" that Rubens add two more articles to the manifest: a horse and a marble table to be deposited with one of the grand duke's own allies at Alicante, on the Iberian coast. What could Rubens do but say yes?

Back at his room in the aftermath, Rubens sent off a dispatch to Chieppio in which he described the meeting in some detail. "I stood there like a dunce, suspecting some informer, or in truth the excellent system of reporters (not to say spies) in the very palace of our prince," he wrote. "It could not be otherwise, for I have not specified my baggage, either at the customs or elsewhere. Perhaps it is my simplicity which causes me astonishment at things that are ordinary at court. Pardon me, and read, as a pastime, the report of a novice without experience, considering only his good intention to serve his patrons, and particularly yourself." If things had not gone according to plan, at least he might try to ingratiate himself with his superiors.

Rubens's plea of naive innocence was disingenuous, for at the very least he should have anticipated what was to transpire at that meeting. He had, in fact, already agreed to take on the grand duke's horse two days earlier, when he was approached by a fellow Antwerp native in Ferdinand's employ. Had he let slip with one too many details during their conversation? Probably not, but the assertion in his letter to Chieppio that he had not "specified" his baggage was patently false. If Rubens was surprised at all, it might have been that the grand duke was willing to trust him with his horse in the first place, given that his journey from Mantua to Pisa had been something of a fiasco from its very outset, and its tortured progress no great secret in the halls of Tuscan power. This was probably on Ferdinand's mind as well, but the audience with Rubens had been called less as a test of the painter's competence than as a message to his Mantuan nephew, Vincenzo. Ferdinand was not prepared to simply cede his role as Italian arbiter of cultural authority to the Spanish crown. Just two years earlier, Ferdinand had sent his own immense gift to Lerma: a marble fountain capped by a statue of Samson slaying a Philistine. This masterpiece was the work of the sculptor Giambologna, himself a Flemish transplant to Italy. Now Vincenzo's gift would pass, but not without Ferdinand's tacit approval.

Rubens's journey from Mantua to Pisa had in fact been such an amateurish farce that any number of sources could have provided Ferdinand with information on its bungled early stages. At Ferrara, the convoy's first stop, customs officials had insisted upon opening for inspection each of the seven trunks in the shipment, not counting the plainly visible horses and carriage. (Rubens, who could be obsessive about his reputation, conveniently neglected to mention this when he had asserted that his luggage had not been inspected.) The Ferrarese presented Rubens with a duty so large that it exceeded the entire projected cost of the trip to Spain. Vincenzo might have sent along a formal request that the cargo be exempted from such levies, but he considered it beneath his dignity to do so; that would have looked cheap. Instead, Rubens was provided with a packet of letters of introduction, and forced to scurry about begging the intercession of local figures of influence with ties to the duke. Acting nimbly, he managed to free the cargo, but the scene was rehearsed again at Bologna, the next stop, where authorities were satisfied by what was generously described as a "tip," and once again in Florence, after an arduous trek over the Apennines.

The drive over the mountains was particularly expensive and time-consuming. Rubens was forced to commission oxen to pull the luggage through the muddy Apennine passes, with their narrow switchbacks and steep inclines. The Tuscan vistas were spectacular—when they were visible through the rain and fog—but the cost for hauling the carriage alone was enormous, and that was without the protective cart built to carry it, which had to be left behind. Upon arrival at Florence, things didn't much improve. When Rubens presented his credentials, he was met by looks of bewilderment. What was he doing in Florence? Why hadn't he taken the direct route from Mantua to the port of Genoa? "They almost crossed themselves in their astonishment at such a mistake," Rubens observed. Instead, incompetent Mantuan court functionaries, perhaps jealous of his mission, had sent him on a circuitous fool's errand southeast through Tuscany, forcing a needlessly difficult mountain crossing. Worse still, he might sit idle and bleeding funds for three or four months waiting for a ship to Spain at Pisa, whereas service out of Genoa was far more dependable.

The delay with the carriage and spring flooding along the route to the coast kept Rubens in Florence for ten days. When he did reach Pisa, at least there was good news: a fleet of ships from Hamburg happened to be in port and en route to Alicante. He booked passage, but now there was an additional problem. It was Rubens's understanding that once he arrived in Spain, the ride to Madrid would take roughly three days. Once again, even a brief glance at a map would have shown quite clearly that on this he had been badly sold by his handlers in Mantua. (No small irony, given that the astronomer and cartographer Giovanni Antonio Magini was a Mantuan court resident and had been working on an atlas of greater Italy for ten years.) The journey was actually some 280 miles—a good two weeks in travel time—and the funds with which he had been provided would not suffice. Vincenzo's precious horses, bathed regularly in wine to maintain their lustrous coats, could not be pressed, lest they appear worn out at their presentation to the king. Frustrated, Rubens wrote to Chieppio asking for additional funds, while promising to spend his own salary until he could be reimbursed. "No one can accuse me of negligence or extravagance; my clearly balanced accounts will prove the contrary," he wrote. "I beg you to favor me by informing His Highness freely of everything, or by having him read this letter." A few moments later he thought better of this presumptuous request and tacked on a postscript: "It would be better for me if you were to make a verbal report; the letter in certain places may exceed the limits of modesty and reverence for His Highness."

The journey across the Mediterranean was slow but uneventful, and for a while it seemed that luck had turned in favor of the young painter. At Alicante, he consigned the horse and table of the grand duke without difficulty. But he also learned that the overland trip across Spain, which was already going to be weeks longer than expected, was to be longer even still. The Spanish court was not in Madrid; since 1601, it had been removed to Valladolid, several days to the northwest over difficult terrain. That shift, which lasted five years, had come at the bidding of Lerma, whose intention was to isolate Philip III from the chattering political busybodies of Madrid, and thereby enhance his own influence.

The trek from Alicante to Valladolid was a twenty-day slog through wind and rain that matched all the difficulty of the crossing of the Italian boot. And when Rubens finally did arrive at the residence of Annibale Iberti, Vincenzo's Spanish ambassador, he was greeted by another surprise. Philip wasn't in town.
